text: To meet this unprecedented level of uncertainty, we will set aside a larger sum in the Contingencies Funds, so that we can respond to urgent and unforeseen needs swiftly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This will allow the Government to respond quickly to any unforeseeable developments arising from COVID-19.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This could include public health or fiscal measures that have to be put in place quickly, if the medical or economic situation deteriorates.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will do our best to avoid this, but we must be prepared for any eventuality.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The use of the Contingencies Funds is subject to proper governance and accountability.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Under the Constitution, the Minister for Finance may make advances from the Contingencies Funds if the Minister is satisfied that there is an urgent and unforeseen need for the expenditure, and the President concurs with the making of such advances.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Thereafter, the amount advanced shall be included in a Supplementary Supply Bill or Final Supply Bill, which will be presented to and voted on by Parliament, as soon as practicable.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This approach is appropriate and prudent, given the fluid situation which may require the Government to act swiftly in the coming months.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: (In Mandarin):   	This is the fourth Budget I introduced this year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Since I presented the Solidarity Budget seven weeks ago, the situation has deteriorated sharply.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many countries have imposed the lockdown measures to control the pandemic, causing an unprecedented impact on economies and societies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: There is still much that the international community does not know about the virus.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is difficult to predict accurately how the pandemic will evolve.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Hence, the road ahead of us is fraught with uncertainties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We need to give targeted support to firms and workers, and to do so in a way that allows our workers and businesses to adapt, transform and pivot towards new opportunities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This allows us to preserve jobs, livelihoods and businesses.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This includes 40,000 jobs, 25,000 traineeships and 30,000 skills training opportunities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This will benefit graduating students and mid-career Singaporeans, enabling them to join the workforce sooner.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Tenants of Government properties will also receive between one to two months of additional rental relief.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: On top of existing rebates, these tenants could receive a total of two to five months of rental rebates.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Hawkers in Government-operated hawker centres or markets can receive a total of five months of rental rebate.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At the same time, we will provide 75% wage support for firms that are not allowed to re-open.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will also increase the wage support for firms that have been more severely hit than expected.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will also provide foreign workers' levy waivers and rebates to firms that cannot re-open.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Digitalisation is increasingly important for firms, especially SMEs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will also provide more support for Singaporeans, set aside resources to encourage philanthropy, so as to build a more resilient and inclusive society.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Every household with at least one Citizen will also receive a one-off $100 Solidarity Utilities Credit.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will also support the social sector in digitalising and scaling up capabilities to better serve their beneficiaries.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Government will also set aside $100 million to provide dollar-for-dollar matching on eligible donations for charities and provide a top-up to the Invictus Fund to encourage Singaporeans to donate generously.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As online communications become more prevalent, the Government will also launch a series of initiatives to partner families and communities to enable more seniors to use digital technologies and enjoy the convenience that these technologies can bring.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have been able to do so because we have our Past Reserves as a strong backing.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Here, I would like to thank President Halimah for giving in-principle support for the Government to draw $31 billion from our Past Reserves to support this Fortitude Budget.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our Past Reserves are accumulated by our forefathers through their hard work.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must cherish it and make every dollar spent count.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Soon, we will be celebrating our 55th National Day.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our forefathers overcame all kinds of difficulties with the spirit of fortitude to build what Singapore is today.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: COVID-19 is a real test for our generation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Although the future is uncertain, if we can adapt to the changing circumstances, respond with fortitude, and unite as one, we shall overcome this crisis and secure our future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, I will now conclude in English.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The COVID-19 crisis is a major challenge for Singapore and all Singaporeans, and for people around the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Singaporeans from all walks of life have responded with unity, resilience and in solidarity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Even as we stay home for Singapore, we take the inconveniences in our stride and make the necessary adjustments to our daily routines with the support of digital tools.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many festivities such as Easter, Vesak Day and Hari Raya Puasa were celebrated virtually.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We continue to resolutely tackle the twists and turns in this COVID-19 pandemic together.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In response to the surge in global demand for masks and export restriction controls on key medical supplies, we are building up the local production of surgical and cloth masks.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are managing the situation in migrant worker dormitories together.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our agencies pulled out all the stops to set up centres in a matter of days and have been running major operations to take care of the workers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: NGOs such as the Migrant Workers' Centre and volunteer groups such as the COVID-19 Migrant Support Coalition are also providing significant support.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many are coming forward to contribute their resources, skills and gifts to help the wider community get through this together.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Arts organisations are developing digital content to keep people engaged at home.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: An example is 3Pumpkins, a community arts company working with local artists to produce programmes for Malay, Mandarin and dialect-speaking audiences, which are then hosted online.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Several Members of this House have also been part of local efforts to hand-sew reusable masks – masks sewn with love.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: CARE officers from Government agencies and volunteer professionals from the social service and private sectors are manning the 24-hour National Care Hotline.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This hotline continues to provide emotional support to those in need during the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many others are finding new ways to bring their communities together.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Even though PA's interest group activities have been suspended, Mr Dick Yip has turned to live-streaming tools to engage new and existing members who share common interests.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The group now meets twice a week – more frequently than before.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This spirit of Singapore Together will be critical as we come together to recover and rebuild for a stronger, more sustainable tomorrow.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As we carefully exit the circuit breaker, we will focus on safely reopening our economy and our society.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I call on everyone to stay the course with the necessary safe reopening measures.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our collective action protects us, our families, our community, our lives.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will continue to bolster our economic resilience.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: During our virtual meeting, the Singapore Business Federation emphasised that businesses must support one another.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our trade associations and chambers (TACs) have stepped up to support businesses.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And of course, landlords can support their tenants.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In the spirit of Singapore Together, I hope Singaporeans will participate and share your ideas.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: On the social front, we will continue building our social resilience.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In this Budget, I spoke about building social resilience through digital inclusion and strengthening our social service agencies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Building a resilient society requires our collective ideas and energy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is about knowing who we are as a people and what we stand for.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In these trying times, we must take special care of the more vulnerable members of our society, be they seniors, individuals with special needs or those who lost their jobs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are implementing many help schemes to meet various needs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some groups have been more severely affected, such as low-wage workers in informal jobs and self-employed persons whose incomes have fallen sharply.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will continue to assist them and help to strengthen their longer-term social security.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our social service agencies, charities and volunteers have stepped up.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Let us mobilise everyone to do our part to build a more resilient Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The battle against COVID-19 will be a long one.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The road ahead will be uncertain, with more ups and downs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Moving forward with fortitude – as we stay united as one people, remain resilient in the face of adversity, and stand in solidarity with one another.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will emerge stronger together as Singapore United, Singapore Together.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.56 pm until 5.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The global situation remains uncertain and we have to expect further twists and turns.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides taking care of the health of our people, jobs are our next foremost concerns.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We know that the human costs would enormous if there are massive job losses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And having a direct bearing on jobs, are business survivability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must prevent large number of businesses failing as it can lead to permanent damage to our economic capabilities, which will have longer term ramifications on livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, in view of the imperatives to save lives, save jobs and save businesses and to also pivot into seizing new opportunities ahead of us, I support the overall allocation of this fourth Budget.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, we are talking about both saving current jobs as well as creating new jobs and traineeship opportunities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would be an uphill task, given the dire global economic circumstance and that the risk of local infections still restrict the normal function of economic activities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Understandably, businesses will take a cautious stance in new hiring.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We can also expect some job loses as more companies run into financial difficulties.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government responded swiftly and in each of the four Budgets extended timely support and assistances to businesses, in areas of cash flow, credit and cost.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The hope is that these relief measures can help buy time for companies and save jobs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And to a very large extent, this has been effective; the situation would have been worst otherwise.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Of course, all these measures also come with a very high fiscal price tag and difficult to sustain in the long run.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The JSS incentivises companies to hold on to their employees.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In return, they received cash subsidies from the Government for up to 75% of most wages.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By receiving direct wage support from the Government, it also obliges the company to do their part to hold on their employees which is the clear intent of the JSS.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is commendable that some companies have come forward to return the JSS back to the Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Others may use the wage subsidy to hire more manpower, which is also as important as it helps to absorb the excess labour in the market.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We hope those companies that can afford to hire, hire more, be it just marginally.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: All these add up to keep up the overall employment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Already, we have read news of companies committing to hiring more workers, some done out of corporate social responsibility.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have to do whatever it takes to avoid structural unemployment from creeping up and taking root within our economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, we must avoid a situation of a lost generation in the making, where young graduates are unable to find employment or being underemployed at this young age.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The public sector will lead by example by creating 15,000 new openings and the Government will help businesses create another 25,000 with a series support measures including hiring incentives.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The other side is to find workers with the required skills sets that can do the job.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here is where we often run into difficulties, matching jobs to the workers with the required skills, especially for PMETs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During the Unity Budget debate, I spoke about the inherent friction a mid-career jobseeker has to go through to make mid-career job changes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is often a strenuous journey that comes with lots of pain points.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The jobseekers often have to contend with employers' biasness or specific preferences, whether it is experience, age and others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The other more complex challenge is a situation where there is no direct match between the jobs that are presently available versus the skills the workers currently have.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We would need to train and right-skills the workers so as to match to the jobs that are available or in demand.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is, of course, a timing issue and also whether we have the ability anticipate the specific skillsets that are needed and set up the relevant training ahead of time.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employers naturally want to hire workers with the relevant experience so that the employees can ideally be productive on day one.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Not an easy problem to solve but the workaround here is to offer on-the-job training by way of subsidised traineeships and programmes such as Attach-and-Train.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And I am glad the Finance Minister has noted this problem and in the fourth Budget, introduced further support and funding for traineeships and training for both recent graduates and mid-career jobseekers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Of course, this would also require employers to be open-minded about workers with no relevant experience and to take a more enlightened and a bigger picture view in the development of their workforce.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are now a whole range of new and existing schemes helping workers to enhance employment and employability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are also a series of initiatives for businesses to help train workers, job redesign, improve productivity and so on.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For all these efforts yield the right outcomes, the stakeholders need to work well together. whether it is their businesses, unions, Government agencies and others and the work cut across different industry, sectors and ITMs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, this is clearly a complex and daunting undertaking – enter the National Jobs Council.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I cannot think of a better person than Senior Minister Tharman to helm this mammoth task.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Senior Miniser Tharman has been instrumental in building up the SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He has in-depth knowledge and experience on the economy and the markets and certainly, the strategic wisdom, gravitas and respect to get the system going.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I am so happy with the choice by the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Safe distancing measures and minimising of physical contacts has changed our way of life and going forward, will change the way we live, work, learn and socialise.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For many years, businesses and governments have been talking about flexi-work arrangements, working from home and BCPs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some even said that employers are mostly lip-servicing and the vision can never be realised.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, COVID-19 has game-changed this in one stroke.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Organisations are thrown into the deep end as governments introduced lockdowns and restrict human gathering and movements.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Businesses are forced to quickly re-configure their operations and workflows and many have to hastily brush up their BCPs so that most of their employees, including management can work from home and alternate sites.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Digital connectivity becomes the life blood to keep businesses and operations going.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And the good news is, offices and operations continue to function despite the tight circuit breaker measures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By and large, companies and employees have adjusted and adapted to the "new normal" of work.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, there are now more legs for an even more extensive flexi-work arrangements going forward.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In area of sales and services, those businesses and retailers with online transactional and service capabilities are able to continue doing businesses despite the circuit breaker measures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Those who have yet to adopt digitalisation, now felt more compelled to gear up their capabilities and devise new digital operating models and solutions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, this is the perfect timing and opportunity to mount a further home-run push for digitalisation for our small businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is a case of all-stars aligned or in Chinese, they called it, 天时，地理，人和, the right time, right place and the right consensus to push for all out digital transformation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This digital push should go beyond businesses and into the social spaces like the neighbourhoods, schools, homes and individuals.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For digitalisation to be part of our lives, everyone should be digitally enabled so that entire eco-system can realise its full potential and to reap the benefits of scale.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, the seniors deserved our utmost attention and our concerted effort.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Recently, I organised e-chit chat with my grassroots seniors' group.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We set up a call link and invited the seniors to join the video call.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They were initially apprehensive and worried that they cannot handle the e-link up.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But come the day of the meeting, I was very pleased to see almost everyone in the call.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Of course, many have their children and their grandchildren by their side to help them to connect, to mute and unmute when they speak.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The seniors told me they thoroughly enjoyed the session as they have not met each other for quite some time and were very glad to see the happy faces around.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They were thrilled that they can speak to each other, see each other at their homes, and even took a group picture.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Importantly, it helps them to overcome the mental barrier about technology and it is not as difficult as they previously thought.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And this is part of the last 5% that I talked about.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many are looking forward to the reopening and exiting the circuit breaker measures in the coming weeks.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we must always bear in mind that the virus is still out there and there is still no vaccine yet to protect ourselves.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, every personal measure that we take to protect ourselves and others must continue.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There may well be new cases as we open up.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I believe that now, we are much better prepared.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Of course, thanks to all our frontline warriors and the Multi-Ministry Task Force.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In a way, there is now certain comfort that we do have the capability and capacity to cope with a steepened infection curve with very low fatality, although we really hope not to be stress-tested again.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, thank you to our frontline colleagues for persevering and battling on, in the most difficult circumstance and for keeping the workers and Singaporeans safe.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is in this uncertain times and very troubling situation that all the more we need a steady hand to steer the ship and a strong leadership that unite us to overcome and forge forward.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I work in the financial sector and I have seen firsthand how the Deputy Prime Minister, when he was helming MAS during the Global Financial Crisis, calmly steered Singapore out of the Global Financial Crisis and in the process, strengthened our position as the premier financial hub.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, I am most reassured that he is now leading the charge with this comprehensive and bold response to overcome the crisis that we are now facing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While there is a need to focus on pumping oxygen into the economy, we must squarely face what the crisis has taught us if we are to truly emerge stronger.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I will then comment on two specific Government measures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As the COVID-19 situation wears on, we are beginning to understand more about the different impact it has on the various segments of society.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In Singapore, we see how the mantra of "stay home and save lives" may actually harm some who are forced to stay home.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As far as work is concerned, we see essential workers outside battling the virus while highly paid persons stay safe at home, being classified "non-essential".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singapore's foreign workers dormitories have become "ground zero" for the battle.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Globally, evidence has emerged that women are disproportionately affected by COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, a United Nations report on 9 April concluded that the COVID-19 pandemic has a "shadow pandemic" exacerbating gender inequality.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Domestic violence has spiked in other countries as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In terms of economic impact, there has been significant employment loss for women, who hold the majority of insecure, informal and lower-paying jobs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The global health workforce is estimated to comprise 67% women, with many women in roles most exposed to the virus.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Unpaid work by women has also increased during this period.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Women are disproportionately affected in other ways too.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, there is growing evidence that female academics are publishing less than male academics during the COVID-19 lockdowns as they are bearing the brunt of family care responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This would clearly impact their careers where publications are a key performance indicator.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Anecdotally, if one looks at Singapore's home-based learning for students, mothers on the whole appear to be spending much more time with their children than fathers, who may also be at home during this period.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: With everyone at home all day, foreign domestic workers face overwork and having inadequate rest.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While men appear more prone to succumb to the virus, it is women and girls who pay the social and economic toll.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The UN urges governments to ensure that their response to the COVID-19 crisis does not intensify the gender inequality crisis.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To that end, one of the UN's key recommendations is to ensure women's equal representation in all COVID-19 response planning and decision-making.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In order to build future resilience for the next crisis, there is a need to study gender-aggregated data in all fields from public health to economics to communications.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Besides gender, any agency looking at long-term recovery should include diverse voices.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is especially necessary to include those familiar with segments that bore a disproportionate brunt of the virus.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This may be a missed opportunity, especially when it has been noted that management of the COVID-19 crisis has been particularly successful so far in Taiwan and New Zealand, with women at the helm.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In my view, the task force could benefit from having more women, especially women who understand gender issues.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Also, there seems to be a weak representation of multiracial voices as there is no Malay member on the task force.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It also does not seem that there is any representation for SMEs as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: With inadequate balance, will the final report and recommendations risk having blind spots that will prevent us from truly emerging stronger as a nation?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The ways of the past may be inadequate or inappropriate today.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, is it time to include more stabilisers in the system?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If there had been schemes such as redundancy or unemployment insurance, the Government may not need to spend as much as it is doing today to support workers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If, for instance, CPF members have some access to their excess CPF funds even before they reach 55, some would not be facing the cliff-edge today.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These are just two examples of what I mean by the task force not being shackled by the models of the past.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While it was an auto-inclusion scheme, it was announced that NTUC would be helping the Government administer appeals from those who were not auto-included.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Questions from the ground have now emerged about the purpose and fairness of the scheme.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As pointed out by my colleague Dennis Tan during the Resilience Budget debate, one issue is what the annual value of the property one lives in has got to do with whether the person has suffered serious income disruption.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is all the more so for those who do not own the properties they live in.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To illustrate, I have several residents who are disqualified from SIRS due to this criterion because they are living in their parents' homes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some of their incomes have dropped to zero as they are service providers for weddings and other events, and will likely not be able to resume their work for months.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Others include freelance music teachers who are unable to conduct physical classes even on a one-to-one basis.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For those who appealed for SIRS, NTUC has partially allowed some appeals.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Suffice to say, these disparate outcomes have caused frustration and feelings of arbitrariness and unfairness.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What are the criteria for allowing or rejecting appeals?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Speaker, SIRS involves public funds – to be exact, SIRS involves the use of past reserves.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Who should be in charge of the scheme?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From the cases we have seen, it is NTUC that is fronting all communications in appeals while the role of MOM is not visible.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From a governance perspective, why was there a need to outsource the administration of SIRS appeals to NTUC in the first place?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Was this done due to a lack of manpower or other reasons?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will this set a precedent for the Government to outsource its schemes to external parties to manage?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was announced in the Fortitude Budget that the Infocomm Media Authority (IMDA) would launch a Seniors Go Digital movement to support seniors to adopt digital channels and hone digital skills.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was highlighted that the inability to connect digitally during the circuit breaker would lead to isolation, which could affect health.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For some years now, well before COVID-19 emerged, the push for a Smart Nation had seen huge efficiencies but also costs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Everyone was channeled towards more and more digital modes of transacting with the Government, whether it be the CPF Board, LTA, or the Traffic Police.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As systems got more sophisticated, citizens were required not only to log in but also to receive one-time passwords or use tokens for added security.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The now default mode of needing SingPass to transact has alienated those who either cannot afford the necessary devices, who do not have the required language skills or who simply cannot wrap their heads around IT environments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To illustrate, I visited a CPF branch office some weeks ago.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I observed the typical scenario of an elderly person with his daughter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: She told him in Mandarin, "爸爸，我们现在去楼上拿SingPass", meaning they had to go to another section to arrange for SingPass.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The elderly man looked totally helpless as he quietly obeyed his daughter's instructions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In this case, the man is fortunate to have a caring daughter to help him navigate an unfamiliar frontier.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But what about those who do not have anyone to rely on?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Or worse, those who place their trust in the wrong people and become victims of crime?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Has technology, instead of empowering them, disempowered them instead?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He described the struggles of those who were illiterate or did not have a mobile phone or computer.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For persons with no income, maintaining a mobile phone subscription is a financial outlay.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is understandable for security reasons but it also means that children could not use their phone lines to transact for their elderly parents, thus requiring more purchases of items simply to transact with the Government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To avoid being misunderstood, let me say that the Seniors Go Digital movement is well-intentioned and I support it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, I hope it will not be approached from the perspective that seniors are somehow "falling behind" and need to "catch up", which would stress them even further.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How will the Government initiatives adapt or customise digital solutions, to design them to be friendly to those who cannot see or hear well, or whose command of English is not strong?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will seniors have low-cost options that are basic in nature?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Can we not simply respect their choice in their old age and always have an option for counter service?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Currently, we are preoccupied, almost bogged down, by the health and economic fall-out of the virus.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, it is necessary to look to building for the future, and to that end, we need to learn from the blind spots that the virus has uncovered, with humility and grace.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Let us not waste this opportunity to amplify the voices of those most affected by the pandemic, in our search for a sustainable recovery.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the easing of circuit breaker measures, some of us are returning to work and school.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But we are certainly not going back to the way things used to be pre-circuit breaker, as COVID-19 is still not behind us.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In the last two months, the priority was to keep everyone safe and ensure that we are able to take care of those who did fall ill.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The need to minimise the risk of transmission and safe distancing has changed the way we work, live and even socialise.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Businesses have not been able to operate as usual with some completely not able to operate at all.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many have not had work as business operations slowed or had to stop during the circuit breaker and others had to take lower pay due to the drop in business demand, while others had to be redeployed and some have lost their jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The various measures with the Unity, Resilience and Solidarity Budgets have been focused on supporting businesses with operating and wage costs with the objective to protect jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The phrase that thes are “unprecedented times” has been used often these last few months.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Indeed, what we are facing is not something any of us could have imagined.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Everyone of us, young and old have had to make painful adjustments.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While we understand the need for these adjustments to keep ourselves and our loved ones safe, they have been tough and for many, jobs and livelihoods have been impacted.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There is much in the Fortitude Budget – I will be touching on two points which is jobs and digitalisation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Businesses large and small, across all industries have been impacted with demand and supply disruptions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This has had a direct impact on jobs and the very nature of how work is done.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Anxiety over employment is felt not just by those whose jobs or incomes have been impacted but even for those who are in employment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There is a fear of further job losses as some businesses have had to close especially in sectors like F&B, retail, hospitality and tourism-related industries.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While some jobs will go away, I do hope that we do not lose heart because new jobs will be created.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am glad that the Budget has given specific attention to providing traineeship opportunities for mid-career workers who have lost their jobs as we all recognise this group of workers find it even tougher, not just in COVID times but even in ordinary times, they find it tougher and they take longer to be able to find employment after they lose their jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What is key is connecting these mid-career workers who have lost their jobs with the opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I hope that Deputy Prime Minister can share more on how mid-career workers can access these opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While the jobs are there, there is lots of information and we need to ensure that the people who need these jobs are well-connected.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While having jobs and opportunities is critical, we must also pay attention to how work is done as the nature of work has changed, given the COVID situation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will mean that as we prepare workers for new opportunities, beyond just upgrading skills, attention needs to be given in terms of how to adopt new ways of working and being productive working remotely.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For some, their first day of work and meeting their new bosses and colleagues will be virtually.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Effectively communicating and collaborating will require skills for one to be effective in their jobs and to be successful.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Even how performance is being measured needs to be taken into consideration.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do want to highlight an area that I think needs attention.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With businesses resuming operations there will be also adjustments for safe distancing measures as well as dealing with the challenges of demand, supply and in some cases manpower disruptions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Attention needs to be paid to working conditions including work hours and workplace arrangements.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Especially for essential services and front-line services, manpower supply may not have fully resumed leading to constraint on manpower.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This could lead workers to have to take on longer working hours.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With requirements for safe distancing measures, businesses must pay attention to also things that ordinarily they would not have to which is even providing places for their workers to have a meal properly in their short break times.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This was not something that employers needed to pay attention to but all this, may be difficult for some companies and the workers' welfare may be compromised.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The reasons cited, of course, were practical ones that included unable to access resources as well as having family members in the house and having to share resources and space constraints.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: One of the factors that was highlighted was also longer working hours.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think attention needs to be paid also to the nature of work and how work is being done because the work environment now is not just in the work place but it is also virtually.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In the last two months, COVID-19 and the circuit breaker measures have accelerated digitalisation faster than one could ever imagine.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There has been a lot of push back of all the areas of digitalisation, both by users, by organisations in terms of policies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But individuals and businesses have had to leverage digital platforms to continue to be able to access services, connect and continue operations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And this has created new habits and new ways of doing things.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Painful as some of it may have been, I think many have seen the benefits.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And so it is a real plus point that digitalisation this COVID-19 has enabled some people and organisations to get past that barrier.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think this is so important to ensure that no one is left behind and more importantly to be able to meaningfully engage and connect to the services and the opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While funding and support is required to go digital, digitalisation has to be more than just about technology.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Going digital is also more than just mirroring traditional ways of doing things.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is an opportunity to reimagine, improve improve and redesign how we do things and enable more to be done.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, let us not waste this opportunity and ensure that this benefit of doing things differently and doing things better through digitalisation is realised for every segment of the population.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is not just about teaching seniors digital skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is about enabling them to connect, enabling them to stay engaged and all the other groups to be able to do the same thing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I really am very happy and very supportive of this programme because, as we all know, while devices are important, funds are important, to drive change you need support, you need engagement and having that with a thousand Digital Ambassadors doing that will make that big difference and will help us get past this, and allow our seniors as well as our hawkers to really fully come on board and be digitalised.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How and when we beat COVID-19 is not certain.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But I do not think it has to necessarily be only when a vaccine is found.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: During these last few months, we have witnessed many examples of the Singapore spirit, generosity as well as our resilience.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I believe that all of us working together as SGUnited will allow us to overcome this crisis and emerge stronger.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Government must provide the leadership, the right programmes and the right policies to build for our future.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Our businesses must rebuild, recover and invest to stay relevant.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Our people will need to stay positive because it is tough, what everyone is going through is tough, but we must stay positive and work together to overcome current challenges and continue to reskill and be ready for the future.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have stabilised the COVID spread in our community, but we still have much to do to overcome significant economic challenges.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Without these Budgets, many more companies would fold and many more workers would be retrenched.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And frankly, we would all be in deeper dire straits.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This money certainly helps but it cannot replace the economic activities to sustain our livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We must therefore brace ourselves for tougher times: wage cuts and inevitable job losses.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But they do tell me that they have conflicting concerns: one, is of course on their jobs and their job security but the other is how can they be safe when they go back to work?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: One, keep the economy open, help the economy re-open and, importantly, keep our economy open by diligently practising safe management measures on the ground.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is the most obvious and the most important thing to do for protecting workers' lives and for opening up the lifeline towards livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Two, while we get our economy back into shape, we need to preserve jobs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We need to create jobs, temporary ones even; and match workers to these new jobs when old jobs are lost.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Make sure that at-risk groups are taken care of.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is the immediate track of things that we must do.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Three, we must make use of the current crisis to push economic transformation.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ironically, as Mr Liang Eng Hwa has mentioned, COVID-19 has sped up disruption and moved us towards Industry 4.0 in double quick time.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Businesses are on a burning platform – it is now "adopt new business models, new technologies" or die.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Workers have taken to digital technology to do their work, order their food and even to keep in touch with family at a faster rate that what was previously not possible.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We must use this transformative track to redesign jobs and create new, Industry 4.0, jobs so that workers, with the appropriate training, can take up these new jobs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The key now, really is to implement this strategy well.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is not sufficient for us to simply know what to do, but to do it well.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Doing so is not only the Government's responsibility alone.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Every business owner and every worker has a shared responsibility and an important role to play.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ms Slyvia Lim spoke about the Self-Employed Persons Income Relief Scheme (SIRS) that NTUC helps to administer.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But, maybe she does not quite remember the history of why we stepped into SIRS in the first place.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Back in January, February, when COVID-19 started to hit.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: NTUC, with our National Taxi Association noticed that taxi drivers' incomes were dropping like a rock.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Because we have some capabilities to augment the Government in extending this help to taxi drivers or freelancers as quickly as possible.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Well, are there things that we can do better?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I think, in time to come when we can settle the immediate issues that we have to deal with with COVID-19 and the transformative things NTUC is embarking on, I will humbly say that, "Yes, we will look at areas where we can do better".

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But, as it stands now, NTUC has extended a care fund to help all workers and likewise, we would like to do our part to help freelancers or self-employed persons deal with the current situation as well.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have put up a Self-Employed Person (SEP) training fund, besides SIRS, to help as SEPs and freelancers upgrade themselves and get into some training in dealing with COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In the course of the three Budgets, NTUC provided feedback to the Government that these are needed things to do.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And I recall, it was a late evening, when MOF called me up and I went to the Treasury Building and was told of the request of the Government to administer SIRS.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I gladly informed MOF that NTUC will take up this role – not because we want to be at the centre of things, but because we thought we had the capability to do our part as a tripartite partner.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: If we look at the National Jobs Council that is set up, should NTUC not be in it?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Should the Singapore Business Federation, the Singapore National Employers' Federation not be in it?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: If all of us are not together in this fight against COVID-19 as a team, then I think we would have lost a capability unique to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Yes, the Government has put up the $100 billion Budget, but I think there is space for business owners, NTUC and the workers to play a part.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We should ride on this strength to execute this strategy that I mentioned, well and to the extent possible remain adaptive and learn lessons along the way.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I am humble enough to say that NTUC could have done better in some of the SIRS things that we have done.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But let us draw those lessons when the time comes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Immediately, now, we want to extend assistance to as many as possible.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: So, NTUC, as I have said, will do our part.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As the economy reopens, workplaces must adapt and change to prevent new infections so that importantly, businesses can continue to stay open under Phase One or in the future, Phase Two conditions.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: If we aggregate over the whole world economy, hopefully we can keep infection rates low and manageable, so that Singaporeans can resume some form of normalcy, some form of new economic life.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is critical to protecting lives and importantly, as COVID-19 drags on, to protecting livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: With this ability to ensure the health of workers, then we can work towards jobs preservation.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Many leaders, across different sectors, told me that without JSS, they really would not be able to keep workers on the payroll, even if workers were willing to do their part to help cut costs to save jobs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Besides JSS, NTUC is also helping businesses access other tools to keep business costs as manageable as possible.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These tools are actually already on the table but are often less well-known and utilised.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In the hotel industry where the impact is very serious, the Food, Drinks and Allied Workers Union worked with Shangri-La's Rasa Sentosa Resort & Spa to send workers for training under the Enhanced Training Support Package.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: A staff, Ms Pohleena, previously worked in the back-of-house in service performance management.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But during this challenging period, she was needed in a front-facing role to take care of Stay-Home Notice guests.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For this role, Ms Pohleena went for training at NTUC LearningHub, topped up on her people skills such as communications, so that she can do her new role.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ms Pohleena remained employed, increased her hospitality skill set and upped her value to her employer as a worker.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The hotel also benefited – not only in having a more skilled worker but enjoyed absentee payroll support as well.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Singapore Aero Engine Services was very proactive in working with the Singapore Industrial & Services Employees' Union early on to make use of the training support.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Aerospace by then was already impacted and they could foresee the further impact of COVID-19 on the industry, so they sent their workers for training.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Sahim Bin Anwar is one of the Technicians who was sent for digital training with NTUC LearningHub.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Sahim's digital knowledge has improved and this helps the company take one more step towards Industry 4.0.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: If you do the mathematics, it will add up to about $1.6 million in terms of absentee payroll support for these companies.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is a win-win situation for both workers and companies.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ultimately, workers get to stay in their jobs, preserve their jobs and companies get help with the payroll and have better skilled workers on hand, poised for the eventual upturn.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In the last three to four months, NTUC Job Security Council has been working hard to match at-risk and displaced workers into available jobs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ms Gina Ng is one beneficiary of the Job Security Council.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: She is a Senior Admin Assistant, working at Fairmont Singapore & Swissotel The Stamford for many years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But due to COVID-19, hotel work was drying up.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The threat of losing her job was real.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our union and the Job Security Council worked with the hotel and found her an immediate match to an organisation that was employing.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Gina was job-matched on a three-month secondment to NTUC FairPrice.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: She is now in the middle of her redeployment, gainfully employed while keeping her salary and job title in the hotel.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As we facilitate job matching, workers must also be willing to adapt and acquire new skills too.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Before Gina was redeployed, she went for training in food hygiene and preparation which brought relevant skill sets and value to NTUC FairPrice.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: While the initial transition was challenging, Gina understood the need to be nimble and was willing to do her part to reskill and upskill.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I spoke to Gina when writing my speech last night.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I asked her if she had anything to tell fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: She said with an audible chirp in her voice, "Stay positive, never give up!

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will overcome." Gina will return to the hotel at the end of her secondment on 13 July, keeping her job, getting a secondment out, staying in the workforce.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But we, in NTUC, also understand the looming challenges ahead and are realistic that there is much more to do to help workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is why I fully support the Government's move to set up the National Jobs Council.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Council will have very important work to drive tripartite efforts to help Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is also useful for companies to co-design the training to support business restructuring and redevelopment for Industry 4.0 so that they can be poised for new and more productive Industry 4.0 ways of doing things.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: NTUC, as I had said, will fully support the National Jobs Council.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: So, for those workers that are at-risk or those workers seeking a job, there is practical help for you.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Besides the immediate task of securing jobs to protect workers, NTUC will continue to partner companies that have the capacity and vision to seize opportunities emerging from the COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Even before COVID-19 hit us, our economy was already embarking on industry transformation brought about by technological disruption.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: COVID-19 has accelerated this disruption and it is clear that those who started transformation early, in fact, are coping better with the COVID-19 challenges today. "Transformation" is not just a buzzword.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And, in fact, COVID-19 has made it even more apparent, more plain that businesses will need to work towards digitalisation and Industry 4.0 practices more urgently.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This will help them position themselves and their workers for new opportunities post-COVID.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: NTUC has been working closely with Temasek companies, amongst some 350-plus companies, to push the Company Training Committees, or CTCs, to move businesses and prepare workers for Industry 4.0.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I want to thank Temasek for this support over the last two years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: NTUC will redouble our efforts to partner companies through the CTC platform, to embark on Operations and Technology Roadmapping, or OTR, to transform.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This will not only help companies chart a course to recovery from COVID-19, it will, importantly, help them identify new growth areas for business, exploit new technologies and create new jobs, better jobs, more productive jobs, even starting now.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is an involved process but companies such as Energizer, amongst quite a few, show how the benefits of the OTR can translate on the ground.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Energizer is bringing in advanced, better technologies for its line machines to increase the precision and the quality of their products.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These machines need better skilled operators who are familiar with the new system overall.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Energizer and the United Workers of Electronics & Electrical Industries worked with one of our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) to curate a specific training programme for their Operators to upskill in this technology and work with these new machines.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These steps helped sustain the Energizer business and, importanly, keep workers gainfully employed in the short term.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But in the transformative track, this will put Energizer on a trajectory ready for Industry 4.0 and for our workers to have more productive jobs, better work prospects emerging from COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ultimately, we in NTUC want to take the best care of our workers, whether they are freelancers or unionised workers, and the best way to do so is for the companies to have better business or economy to be able to generate growth, and for workers to have the necessary training and skills to access these jobs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: So, it is not just for the immediate things that NTUC is busy with; even as we are helping workers cope with COVID-19, we are casting our vision further ahead and doing practical things to help companies transform to benefit workers now and in the future.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: (In Mandarin):   I announced in February this year that we are setting up the NTUC Job Security Council to match workers, who are at-risk of losing jobs, to companies that are hiring.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We had over 4,000 companies on board the Job Security Council then.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Companies in the Job Security Council are still hiring, from sectors such as the Healthcare, Transport and Logistics, Built Environment, as well as Electronics and Transport Engineering.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are redoubling our efforts to help these companies find new employees; and more importantly, match our workers to these companies and earn an income.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The National Jobs Council, with Senior Minister Tharman as Chairman and Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat as Advisor, held its first meeting yesterday to discuss how we will help Singaporeans benefit from the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: NTUC will help all workers, whether you are a fresh graduate or mid-career professional, to take advantage of these nearly 100,000 jobs and training opportunities so that you will not only earn an income but gain from training and work experiences.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Chinese word "危机" (for "crisis") consists both "danger" ("危") and "opportunity" ("机").

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The most important thing is that we must remain positive and be nimble.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The key now is to implement this plan well.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These are not easy tasks but we will do our very best.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And only if we can continue the trust and the solidarity of tripartism, then we can overcome.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I have clarification for Minister Ng Chee Meng.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: And Minister Josephine Teo in the right time can answer this arrangement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Just to chime in on what Secretary-General Ng Chee Meng shared earlier, I cannot help but emphasise that this Budget, I particularly like and applaud it because of its focus on workers – the actual focus on the lives and livelihoods of our workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: That is something that struck me very hard.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I wrote an opinion piece, which was published last Saturday in The Straits Times.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This opinion piece came about and these horror stories came about because of the many engagements I had in the last eight weeks of circuit breaker with many union leaders, unionists, residents including fellow workers, through various platforms.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In fact, it is quite a learning journey.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I have been using Zoom, Webex, BigMarker, Microsoft Teams and through various platforms including Facebook Live and LinkedIn Live.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It was a good opportunity to learn those skills but also a fantastic opportunity to engage a lot of workers that I have never had the opportunity to do during normal times because of various constraints and situations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: A second horror story that often plays out that I hear from workers is a situation where a worker, suddenly, during this particular period, gets a very poor performance rating, and previously, he had always had a satisfactory or better rating in the past couple of years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Therefore, his exit from the company is expedited.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The third scenario or story that I hear about is also a situation where employee is given a new job scope, do something very different from what he used to do, or sometimes, even excluded for meetings and important company events.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: And, therefore, in a way, the worker is forced to exit the company.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The fourth scenario happens, as I shared earlier during Question Time, where workers are being contractually terminated, whether with or without notice.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Another scenario or horror story we hear is also of safe workplaces.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Just as recent as we reopened a couple of days ago, I also hear of workers who actually, in their course of work, can or are able to work from home, but are forced to go back to the companies by the management or employers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These are some of the horror stories we have come across.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fortunately, these are not rampant and many of these cases that workers shared about, whether through various platforms, private messages, emails or even conversations that I had in various platforms, most of these happened in many of the non-unionised companies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In unionised companies, we have the collective agreement as well as a lot of negotiation and discussion with companies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: So, we do see quite a bit of these scenarios happening.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am glad that MOM, where they detect such cases, would take resolute steps to enforce against such errant or recalcitrant employers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There is a few that have been rolled out, in particular, to address the COVID-19 scenarios.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Of course, as we reopen and as we go into Phase One, Phase Two, Phase Three, the various scenarios and new normal or next normal, so to speak, that will happen.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I urge employers, in particular, to watch out for all these various advisories to ensure our workplaces are safe for their workers as well as for their customers and clients that visit the workplaces or offices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: More importantly, the tripartite partners really should use this opportunity and will use this opportunity to work even more closely together because this is an opportunity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is a great time, particularly, with all these practices, and a lot of rules and advisories are coming out hard and fast for everyone to work very, very closely together.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At the company level, the trust between employer and employee is very important.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I cannot emphasise more the importance of regular open, transparent communication between employers and employees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
