text: I think this is the best time to build that trust because, not just the affected workers, but those who are not affected, are actually looking at how the employer is treating their employees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: And thirdly, I think I cannot emphasise more, as what Secretary-General Ng Chee Meng mentioned earlier, the need for tripartism and the ability to work as a tripartite front and as a tripartite relationship.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: So, that is one area – sharing some of these horror stories that are happening at workplace which I hope will be eradicated.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am glad that through the SGUnited programme and the whole plethora of programmes that we have had.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The fact that we are faced with challenges – with global lockdowns across various parts of the world and even with our neighbours – it is very important for us to relook not just self-sufficiency in many fronts, but also building and strengthening the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is a great opportunity for us to work together, to build and strengthen and hire and develop Singapore Core – which has always been our agenda in the last couple of years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We have rolled out a series of measures in this area.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We have the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: But it is important for employers to keep their minds open and be open to strengthening the Singaporean Core in all areas, in particular, in that space where there are a lot of professionals, managers and executives (PMETs).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At this point, I would just like to highlight the plight, anxieties and fears of many of our mid-career workers, in particular, the PMETs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: If you look at the global financial crises, be it SARS and even before this entire COVID-19 saga, if you look at the labour market statistics, in terms of the increase in unemployment rate, this particular group, the mid-career workers, including PMETs, are the most vulnerable and most affected.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The increase has been highest in both crises.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: And therefore, I cannot emphasise more the many fears and anxieties.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Even prior to COVID-19, they were already a very vulnerable and susceptible group of workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: But in this Fortitude Budget, I just like to give my thanks and support for some of the things that have been rolled out.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Besides the SGUnited Traineeships and SkillsFuture Traineeships, also the hiring of local workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These are good and resolute measures to help and encourage those companies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I think those that are, are a small group.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I hope we can build the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I hope also that we can pay particular attention to the mid-career workers – even before this entire saga, they were already very vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I hope for more emphasis and more support for this particular group so that they will be able to rise up to the challenge.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As we all slowly reopen, like they say, the many "Rs" – as we renew, as we restart, as we refresh, as we rejuvenate ourselves during circuit breaker for some – let us reinvent ourselves, let us reinvigorate, rejuvenate ourselves so that we are able to reposition ourselves and ensure that in all things that we do, we reforge that trust between the employee and employer; not just an employee-employer, but the employer and his industry; the industry needs to work together and hunt as a pack.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My fellow Labour Members of Parliament have touched on – and others will continue to emphasise – the importance of job creation, job matching and the need to save jobs during this unprecedented period.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In China, over a 100 million people face renewed lockdown in the northeastern region.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In Japan, Hokkaido suffered a second wave of coronavirus infections after lifting lockdown measures while in South Korea, new clusters have formed quickly after lockdown restrictions were eased, forcing closures of more than 250 schools last week, just days after they reopened.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Is this a case of too much, too soon?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With lives and livelihoods at stake, it is not an easy balance to make.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But I would like to urge that we take a more careful and more calibrated approach to prevent this from happening in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Sometimes, new requirements are issued just days after an earlier set of instructions; while other times, they see other businesses implementing these rules quite differently from them.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The mandatory use of SafeEntry is one such example.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Most companies practise the check-in function but, as we know, some do not require you to check out when leaving the premises.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Others provide a barcode reader to allow visitors to scan their NRIC as an alternative, but this is not practised universally.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Should safe management measures be implemented based on principles or should they be prescriptive?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the ground, it seems that bosses prefer to implement based on principles while staff who are tasked to implement the measures prefer a more prescriptive set of instructions for clarity and ease of implementation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Whichever the approach, safe management measures must not inadvertently cause poor safety at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While we can understand that the aim of these measures is to minimise unnecessary social gatherings at the workplace, some types of work do require clear communication and coordinated teamwork.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Keeping a "safety distance" and speaking through a mask could result in unclear communication, which may lead to heightened risks of workplace accidents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For manual work that requires heavy lifting, for example, in the construction or marine engineering sectors, wearing a mask could affect their physically demanding work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, we read last month that the safe distancing dividers on a lorry transport for workers were deemed "not sturdy enough" and could have caused more harm in the event of a traffic accident!

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope MOM can conduct regular reviews and inspections, especially for high risk sectors, and ensure that the safe management measures are working as intended.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many businesses are already reeling from the increasing costs of putting in place the ever-evolving set of protective measures to keep our workplaces safe – providing thermometers and masks, increasing the frequency of cleaning and disinfection, employing additional staff to control access and to monitor temperatures, even increasing the number of trips to ferry workers because of safe distancing requirements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Coupled with a sharp decline in revenue, our businesses are hit with a double whammy!

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many employers that I spoke to are now concerned about the costs of having to send their workers for swab tests as we continue to ramp up community testing.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They tell me that the cost of a swab test seems to vary significantly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Online checks reveal that a swab test can range between US$1 in Senegal to more than US$3,000 in America!

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To manage costs, many businesses are leveraging technology to make our workplaces safer during this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In China, AI-powered thermal cameras are used to identify those in a crowd who have a fever and facial-recognition systems are deployed widely to identify those not wearing masks.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some isolation wards in China are entirely manned by robots that take the patient's temperature, deliver food and medicine and perform disinfection tasks.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, we read that the use of disinfectant tunnels can cause serious harm to those walking through them.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Experts have cautioned against atomising and spraying copious amount of disinfectant on a person as this may cause irritation and potentially irreversible damage to the cornea, skin and even our respiratory system.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many have adapted to working from home in the past two months and I encourage companies to use this opportunity to reinvent their business operations and where possible, embrace work-from-home arrangements permanently and seize the new opportunities that come with this new normal.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our hawkers and wet market stallholders have shown that this is possible.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: During the circuit breaker, many hawkers have united to embrace e-commerce and food delivery.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: IMDA also taught stallholders from Tekka Market how to sell their produce using Facebook live-stream.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, many stallholders have started to live-stream on their own and have been successful in selling their produce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The reinvention of our wet market stallholders to become "web market superstars" shows us that we can all adapt to and seize opportunities in this new normal.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Graduating students and retrenched workers are finding it hard to find a job.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Matured workers are worried about keeping their jobs, while frontline workers fear getting an infection from prolonged exposure during work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even young parents are struggling between balancing their work, helping their energetic children with home-based learning and taking care of their restless elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Having a mentally healthy workforce is important as compliance to safety at the workplace may be compromised if workers are not able to focus at work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I therefore urge the Government to invest more resources on mental healthcare as insufficient support in this area could lead to dire consequences, especially in this prolonged period of uncertainty, anxiety and fear.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that the Government could revisit my numerous proposals to mandate a WSH representative in every company.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us retain and expand the role of these mandatory SMOs beyond the pandemic so that our workplaces can be safer and our workers healthier.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To tide through this pandemic and emerge stronger, we need to rally together as one people.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government has done much to protect lives and livelihoods through an unprecedented series of four Budgets over four months.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Businesses are also doing their part to put in place measures to keep our workplaces and our workers safe.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The onus is on each of us to take care of ourselves and to take care of each other as we resume "Business Unusual".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I call on the Government, all employers and workers to continue to partner with the Labour Movement so that together, we can save jobs and keep jobs safe, because every worker matters.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I rise to affirm my support for the recently delivered Singapore Fortitude Budget Statement and to provide a response from the business and manufacturing community.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As we prepare to exit the circuit breaker, it is again very reassuring to the business community that the central focus of the Fortitude Budget is the protection and creation of jobs.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This unprecedented level of financial relief continues to demonstrate the Government's unwavering commitment to support our enterprises.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As I stated before in my response to the earlier Budget Statements, businesses cannot take these support measures for granted and must actively take steps to continuously examine and tweak their business models and explore how new improvements can be incorporated sustainably.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Manufacturers here are generally very appreciative of the relief measures that will help to ease commercial financial challenges.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Ranging from sustained foreign worker levy rebates and waivers as well as more robust rental relief measures to training of employees and upgrading of equipment, the SMF is thankful that the Government has largely taken on board the feedback of our members in announcing a progressively more comprehensive relief package.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Our members are also heartened that on a government-to-government level, Singapore is working with other countries to keep supply chain disruptions as minimal as possible during this time.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This has significantly helped businesses continue operations during the circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As we take the required steps to exit the circuit breaker and work towards the new normal, I would like to share some feedback on challenges faced by businesses and encourage sustained and greater collaboration within the tripartite alliance.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: On safe distancing and shop floor hygiene – Singapore first became acquainted with the COVID-19 virus early this year and since then, most companies have had to adapt processes significantly to safeguard the health of employees while they struggle with the numerous external impacts on their businesses.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to cleaning costs, companies are now maintaining their own inventory of personal protective equipment (PPE) that is likely to be required in daily operations for an extended period of time.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As such, manufacturers largely expect these costs to be permanent additions to their operational costs.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, the current necessity of remote work also presented significant costs for businesses to introduce mobility into their business models such as required laptops, setting up of remote servers, cloud access and so on.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, we have seen a number of companies modifying their shop floor to comply with safe distancing guidelines.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: All of these costs give rise to genuine concerns of the manufacturing community as to how Singapore can continue to be competitive globally as different countries practise different precautionary measures.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: One of Singapore's advantage has always been speed and efficiency.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: While businesses understand that there is an ever important need to care for the safety and health of our people, businesses here hope that law and policy makers take into careful consideration the need not to be overly prescriptive and at the same time, ensure that regulatory bodies are sufficiently resourced and staffed so that required approvals do not become the bottleneck to efficiency.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: On manpower concerns – the circuit breaker has also presented a wide number of manpower challenges to companies.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Key among which is the uncertainty of the permitted workers' quota, which changes day to day for some companies.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The feedback from member companies is that such fluctuations are an added form of disruption as they are unable to plan ahead and schedule production schedules.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This also has resulted in a core group of the workforce being stretched during this time as many find themselves taking up dual roles.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Such also has a serious impact on manufacturers as they abide by safety standards and regulations, but staff fatigue is always an ever present danger.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Aside from being a key part of the workforce, some Malaysian workers who have chosen to remain in Singapore have been apart from their families for an extended period of time and these form mental welfare concerns for employers.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses know that this is not dependent on Singapore alone.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Accordingly, businesses wish for the governments of both countries to expeditiously reach an agreement to facilitate trade.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Many are worried that the longstanding relationships they have built over the years with customers and suppliers, especially those from overseas, lost during the circuit breaker, may be difficult to woo back.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Many of our members who trade internationally are especially concerned regarding their contractual obligations to overseas clients and that failure to fulfill the same could mean exposure to financial and reputational damages.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that the relevant Ministries can assist to see how some of these issues can be even more quickly resolved.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I will now like to move on to the next part of my speech – that of digitalisation and training.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: On protecting livelihoods, transforming businesses – as president of the SMF, a common refrain when I engage with our members is the need for digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: While the challenges presented by the measures to combat COVID-19 have indeed spurred on digitalisation and transformation for businesses, there is still much to be done.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The SMF administers the Digital Project Management Services programme as part of the SMEs Go Digital initiative.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: While many companies understand the need to transform, a number of concerns still hinder the adoption process.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, the SMF is really glad and heartened that the Fortitude Budget pays importance towards incentivising and encouraging businesses to digitalise.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: We believe that the measures will go some way to pushing companies to take the plunge.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The SMF will also be doing its part to complement that of Government's efforts to push for our members to take up digital solutions on an expedited basis.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, companies seeking to send employees for training during this period have also encountered some challenges that warrant some attention.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: One of the new initiatives under the Fortitude Budget is provision of training opportunities for the older workforce.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: For the manufacturing sector, the transformation journey is one we are committed to and while the change will not be overnight, I strongly believe that our continued efforts as a community will set us on the right path.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: On importance of the tripartite alliance – Mr Speaker, Sir, as I close my speech today, I would like to invite the hon Members of this House to spend some time to ponder on the delicate balance of our labour relations in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I have, in my previous speeches, always made it a point to drive awareness and encourage the strengthening of our unique tripartite labour alliance.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, it is in trying times like these that the true work and importance of this alliance shines more brightly than ever before.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Amid the massive global economic upheaval, with the strength of our labour relations built up over decades, our workers are able to keep faith with their employers and employers are able to keep faith in the Government.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This foundation has provided important stability for our economy during this crisis.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is therefore critical and timely, that as hon Members of this House, we remember and keep this delicate balance in view even as we canvass the interests and views of the organisations we represent.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: During such times of heightened uncertainty and anxiety, it is easy for a statement, though innocuously made, and, perhaps in support of one stakeholder, to engender feelings of negativity or suspicion in another.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is therefore important that in the current circumstances, that we keep communication channels open and transparent between workers, employers and the Government.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: After all, we are all working collectively towards a common goal of emerging stronger as a nation after this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is therefore exceedingly crucial that we continue to be ever mindful of how we can continue to build up such relations.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: May we be in the best possible position to better seize opportunities presented when the effects of COVID-19 recede globally.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I stand in unequivocal support of the Fortitude Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: COVID-19 has taken a heavy toll on the economies of many countries.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In Singapore, the recent circuit breaker has affected many businesses.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We all have friends who have lost their jobs, or their businesses or are struggling in some way.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is a battle not just against COVID-19 but against some of the toughest enemies of any small state – despair, poverty, haplessness, an overwhelming sense of pessimism.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Large states have deeper resources, a stronger pull on world affairs and a sense of control and destiny.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore has always been a price-taker in world affairs and remains vulnerable to all the ugly forces that have come to the fore in this pandemic and we have seen this played out in many countries including Singapore.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What has come out quite starkly is the fact – a fact that we have always known, but perhaps forgotten – that we ourselves must defend Singapore, defend our laws, our rules, our way of life.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We ourselves must call out rule breakers who mock us and write home to invite their countrymen to do the same; we must think of solutions when countries where we locate our assets count their own interests above ours; in times of trouble, we must call our own home from all over the world – as our universities did to thousands of students overseas.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Some of them did bring home the virus and were rightly cared for in our hospitals.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We are our best hope, and we must stand together.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If we break, this dark time will not end and it will be sometime before we see more sunny days and blue skies.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We are slowly but surely emerging out of the circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Today, I would like to share the efforts of our other various entities at NTUC Enterprise who are continuing to address the key concerns of job security and opportunity, and initiatives to moderate the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I declare my interest as the Group CEO of NTUC Enterprise and NTUC FairPrice.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: FairPrice Group has continued to operate our supermarket branches – on line and off line; our hawker centres, foodcourts and coffeeshops; as well as at our warehouses and central kitchens – working hard to meet consumers’ food and grocery needs and adapting to the evolving circumstances daily.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: These efforts help to ensure that the public have access to their daily essentials.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: On a side note, I must declare that Fairprice Group has a food services division through our Kopitiam and FoodFare outlets.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I wish to make a call out for all those in the F&B sector.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, earlier hon Member Mr Lim Biow Chuan made the same call.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Those in the F&B sector have indeed been very badly hit in this crisis because the dining in crowd is a very, very important component of their overall business model.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, whilst the various support schemes by Government have been indeed very helpful, this is but a stop-gap measure and so the earlier we can provide guidance and clarity for the F&B sector, and in particular to ensure that the various measures and reliefs that Government has announced that they accrue and are received by the F&B operators in its entirety.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As is, we can expect more F&B firms to exit this industry and with it, a lot more job losses.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Of course, there will be businesses which are less affected by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For such organisations, they should always remember to recognise the people that make up the organisation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, like others in the essential services, FairPrice group has given special monetary awards and incentives to our colleagues, especially those working at the frontline.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Many customers have also joined us in appreciating our service staff through testimonies on social media as well as through personal cards and letters of encouragement.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Ms Ng was from the Fairmont Singapore and Swissotel.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Besides Fairmont, we at FairPrice group also managed to get staff from Grand Hyatt, Orchard Hotel, Ritz Carlton, Changi Airport Group, Wildlife Reserves and several others to help us out.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Next, let me cover what we have done in terms of commitment to learning.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC LearningHub continues to make learning accessible during this period.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In addition, LearningHub has provided opportunities for self-employed persons to earn as they train to deepen or acquire new competencies, all this in preparation for when the economy picks up and new opportunities arise.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Completion rates of these courses were very encouraging and significantly higher than the industry benchmark.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For the last two months, I think these have all been very well used by parents of such children.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our MoneyOwl too conducted more online webinars and e-learning to educate the public on financial planning and management.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Whilst jobs continue to be a major concern for all, we were also kept busy keeping our operations running and services accessible, and at the same time, doing our best to keep cost of living in check.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And, in fact, this week we started a priority queue for healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And then there were the mobile grocery vans which brought essential products to residents in selected areas without them having to venture too far away from home.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our sourcing teams continued in overdrive mode as we strengthened our network of suppliers across the globe to mitigate any disruptions in supply especially that of essential items.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Efforts to contain COVID-19 will be a long and protracted one.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Labour Movement has always looked after workers and their welfare.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For today, I am highlighting two areas only – jobs and cost of living.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We pledge to ensure stable jobs, affordable groceries, quality and value meals.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As a group, we will continue to do our part for the community through our corporate giving, whether it is donations to vulnerable and community groups or providing more relief to needy families and workers during this difficult period.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is very much part of our DNA and what the public has grown to expect and can expect the NTUC group of Social Enterprises to continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We are finalising these measures and will share with the public soon.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Secretary-General Mr Ng Chee Meng indeed will be the one, together with a few of us, to launch this.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Yes, in the best of times, we cared less for bread and butter – opting for sashimi and salmon.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We aim for high pay and long holidays.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Today, travel, dining out and shopping seem like a dream from the past.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We made a nation out of nothing but gumption and a Separation Agreement.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our first meals were from lean tables; and we can today, endure and grow from these hard times to strength and prosperity.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The sun will shine on Singapore again, but we must ourselves first break through the darkness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Since MTI’s last review in March, the disruptions to economic activity in major economies around the world have been more severe than expected due to the stringent containment measures taken by various governments to slow the spread of COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Most of the major advanced economies as well as the emerging economies are now projected to see full-year recessions in 2020.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Against this backdrop, the outlook for the Singapore economy has weakened further.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The implementation of circuit breaker measures to contain the COVID-19 virus in Singapore was necessary but it has also created an impact on our economy – business operations were disrupted and non-essential business services were forced to close during the circuit breaker period; workers have to make alternative arrangements to work from home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: While we have managed to flatten the epidemic curve, we must now shift our focus to tackle the "unemployment" curve as retrenchment and job losses will inevitably rise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As the Executive Secretary of the Metal Industries Workers’ Union (MIWU), I had the chance to speak with many of our employer partners as well as our workers on the ground.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: They were seeing reduced work hours, shorter work weeks and even no-pay leave is becoming more frequent now in many of our branches and our partner companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, naturally, I understand that our union leaders and workers are concerned about their job security in the immediate and longer term.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Therefore, the Labour Movement welcomes the Fortitude Budget that supports the gradual reopening of our economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The enhancement to the Jobs Support Scheme will help to sustain companies in the early phase of reopening and reduce the pressure to retrench workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: PMETs and workers, aged in the 40s to 50s, are expected to be more impacted by any retrenchments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: They are more likely to face difficulties in finding jobs in this distressed job market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is very much welcomed by union leaders and workers that I spoke to.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The National Jobs Council chaired by Senior Minister Tharman will oversee this effort.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NTUC hopes that the NJC will leverage the NTUC Job Security Council set up earlier in February this year to pre-emptively match at-risk and soon-to-be displaced workers into available job opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These jobs were mainly in essential services or to support COVID-19 efforts, especially in sectors such as healthcare, retail and logistics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Through this, and with the help of many of our unions and the various Company Training Committees (CTCs), NTUC stands ready to support the Government in the National Jobs Council, leveraging our existing capabilities and our network to help match workers to new jobs and also to equip them with deeper skills at the national level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I hope policy incentives being considered by National Jobs Council can further support the early success of NTUC Job Security Council and encourage more companies to join us in this network to create more traineeship placements and more job opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: One of the key enablers to allow better job matching is skills training to ensure our workers acquire future-ready and industry relevant skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: During this economic slowdown, NTUC has been working closely with our unions to encourage companies to send their workers for training and to take advantage of the various schemes, like absentee payroll, for example, to help defray wage costs when the workers are away on training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Companies should also leverage on the CTCs to identify skills and training needs to better upskill their workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is an unionised company under Metal Industries Workers Union (MIWU).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Together with the union, the company set up a CTC in 2019, with the aim of furthering workers' career prospects through relevant skills training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The company engaged NTUC's e2i or the Employment and Employability Institute, to redesign the jobs and raised productivity of their workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Many companies like DKA in the manufacturing sector has been impacted by disruption to the Malaysian workers commuting across from the Causeway due to the lockdowns and the situation in Malaysia.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And by cross-skilling their workers, they are able to respond to this transient manpower shortages and cope with the skill gaps that they may have.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Some companies have pivoted to other business segments with growth opportunities and accelerated their business transformation during this period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: One example is Certact Engineering, a unionised company under MIWU as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This company has recently transformed their business from a plastic and aluminum manufacturing company, to manufacture medical equipment components like the COVID-19 test kits and ventilator component parts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To support the new business requirements, Certact had to remodel their business processes, redesign existing jobs and send their workers for training to operate their new manufacturing lines.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, even as I speak today, Certact is partnering NTUC to leverage the CTC and Operations Technology Roadmapping (OTR) process to implement their new business model and strengthen their workforce capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It allows us to conduct such processes even with circuit breaker measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will be conducting more virtual-OTRs with the various CTCs using online platforms to ensure that companies' transformation needs and workers' training needs continue to be served by the virtual-OTR during this pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Workers have also shared with me that training-related costs may deter their employers facing cashflow challenges during COVID-19 pandemic from undertaking skills upgrading for their workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I want to encourage more companies, both unionised and non-unionised, to approach NTUC to set up CTCs and tap into the additional funding support to send their workers for training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have in place structures and initiatives to help the Singapore economy recover.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Labour Movement also stands ready to journey with our tripartite partners through this challenging period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will continue to work closely with our tripartite partners to keep our workers in jobs, to enhance job matching and job creation for our workers, to encourage skills training so that we can collectively navigate through the new post-COVID era.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Tough times do not last but tough people do.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And I believe that if we continue to stay united, band together, face the challenges head-on as One United Singapore, we will be able to go through this global pandemic together and be ready when the upturn comes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With that, Sir, I stand in support of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thankfully, many received support in various forms during this period.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unfortunately, their income continues to be severely affected.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To assist SEPs cover their immediate and future needs, I have three proposals to make.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are: support to mitigate income drop, support for licensing and accreditation and support in finding new income sources.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A case in point is with the two largest groups of SEPs in Singapore, namely, taxi and private hire drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Together, the National Taxi Association and the National Private Hire Vehicles Association, the Point-to-Point operators and MOT worked out several solutions to deal with a severe drop in passenger numbers and earnings.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But this is a time where we collaborate and work together.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And, as a result, we were able to pool our resources and swiftly rolled out rental rebates and financial aids to drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We, in the NTUC, were also able to extend further assistance to those who were union members.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On their part, I am very grateful to the Point-to-Point operators who gave additional support such as rental waiver, which means they did not collect a single dollar in rental during the circuit breaker period from the taxi drivers and rental reductions even after the circuit breaker period has ended.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Drivers I spoke too are deeply appreciative of the various support given.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: MOT has also supported not just full-time drivers but part-time drivers as well.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We handled the administration because we know the ground and could handle the appeal process swiftly.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As takings are unlikely to return to pre-COVID levels anytime soon, the Ministry has extended the Special Relief Fund to help full-time drivers with rental costs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But the Driver Care Fund has not been extended for part-time drivers who are also struggling.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope MOT and MOF can consider giving part-time private hire drivers a second tranche of Driver Care Fund and to review the eligibility criteria and allow more drivers to qualify.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Those who do not meet the criteria have submitted applications.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Understandably, many SEPs who are not in the auto-qualify group are anxious.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One common issue they face is the lack of a licensing regime to verify if they are SEPs and whether they are struggling with a severe drop in income.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many also had not been diligent in contributing to their MediSave or filing their income tax returns.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This added to the lack of information to verify their status.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Previously, in this House, I have appealed for more groups of SEPs to be issued with a licence.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have also called upon the Government to offer co-contributions to help them contribute to their MediSave.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, SEPs, such as private hire drivers and tour guides hold a vocational licence and are contracted with an operator.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That allowed accurate identification of those who have suffered a severe drop in income.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, those SEPs who are registered with the unions could grant and gain immediate access to help offered by the NTUC.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This covers people such as those who in the National Instructors and Coaches Association who are dealing mainly with people who are sports instructors and coaches offering services.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, we do not yet have a licensing regime for people such as tuition teachers, photographers, performers, dancers, riggers, sound system men in the self-employed group.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Whether it is to offer financial assistance or training help, much effort is needed to ensure that genuine freelancers in need are identified and assisted.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, I would like to propose that MOM spearhead a whole-of-Government approach to have more groups of SEPs issued with a vocation licence or to form accredited professional guilds or join the union.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will allow for proper assessment of their professional needs and provide them with support during a downturn.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The NTUC has, in the past, formed unions for different groups of SEPs and we stand ready to work with the Government to do more.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Only then will guilds be effective and more SEPs see a need to join.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This has been my experience as an advisor with the union, working together with the Point-to-Point Operators and MOT.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because of the strong tripartite relationship, we were able to deliver strong support swiftly to many taxi and private hire drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My other union colleagues shared the same experience when they work with the travel operators and MTI to help our tour guides.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Moving forward, we must ensure that more SEPs can benefit from such a tripartite arrangement.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, I would like to repeat my call for a one-off co-funding by the Government to self-employed persons who make voluntary contributions to their MediSave.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will also go towards ensuring that more of them will be able to save up for their immediate and future medical needs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And finally, we also need to look at ways to help self-employed persons find new sources of income.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The recently announced National Jobs Council is indeed a further boost to this effort.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are sectors that are still hiring and the most pressing task now is to quickly acquire the skills needed and match workers to those vacancies.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But are our self-employed persons ready and have the appropriate mindset to make such switches?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The drivers learnt the skills of engaging customers on delivery matters, use cashless payment and even made adjustments to their daily routine – no more do they queue outside at the airport, but outside of restaurants or supermarkets in order to collect the delivery on time.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To support them, I hope that the National Jobs Council can look at enabling more self-employed persons attain more vocational skills and to earn income from various channels.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This way, our scarce manpower can be better deployed across various industries.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It will also support self-employed persons reduce their downtime through matching them with various assignments.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There may be concern that this multi-skilling of self-employed persons would eat into the domain of other trades.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But the COVID-19 pandemic has already compelled even countries to relook at their longstanding economic strategy and even geared up to becoming less reliant on others.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, we must help reduce the risks self-employed persons face, support them to acquire new skills and leverage on digital tools to optimise their access to work assignments.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Experts are predicting that the way we live, work and play will be very much different post COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We experienced some of this possible new normal during the circuit breaker period.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a nation, we were united, we showed resilience, we fought in solidarity, we strengthened our fortitude.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We know we need to reduce our dependence in some areas and at the same time, develop new mindset and capabilities for us to live, work and play in the new normal.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This current crisis has forced many to re-think on the value that our society has placed on essential service workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The services provided by these workers are truly useful, necessary and the impact will be felt if the work is not done.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unfortunately, in many societies, the more useful the work is, the less they pay you.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, this crisis has caused some to change their attitude and behaviour, and we have witnessed many more people who are being gracious, generous and grateful for the work of our essential service workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC, together with our affiliated unions and associations, have long championed the cause of our low-wage essential service workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To us, every worker matters and every job counts.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While I am heartened that we have made good progress in terms of pushing for better wages and skills, there is much more to be done.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In post COVID-19, what would be the new normal for essential service workers in the outsourced sectors that keep Singapore safe, clean and green?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a society, if we truly value the work of our essential service workers, then it is time for all stakeholders to be bold and embrace change in the new normal.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the new normal, we must change how we treat our essential service workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must continue to find ways to narrow the income gap and ensure their average wage growth continue to be higher than the median.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The tripartite committees overseeing these essential services must work together to enhance the skills and wage ladders to ensure our workers continue to remain relevant and due recognition be given for the importance of their work.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the new normal, we need a PWM where these essential services would be anchored by a skillful and productive workforce, balanced with both the young and old.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Attracting a younger or more skillful workforce has always been a key outcome desired under PWM and to achieve this, we must change how we do things by leveraging technology and digitalisation to support higher productivity and sustain higher wages to attract younger Singaporeans to be essential service workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As there will be older workers in these sectors, we also need to drive a change in our mindset.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must inculcate in all workers a growth mindset where one is never too old to learn new things.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to encourage them to embrace technology to make the work safer and smarter.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Changing the way we do things for the future is already mapped out in the different Industry Transformation Maps for the respective essential services industries.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This plan must be reviewed for the new normal.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to change the assumptions when these plans were developed to accelerate the transformation of the industry for the new normal where we drive productivity increase through technology and digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: All of this require a highly skilled workforce and the new PWM must reflect the changes in skills and productivity required to justify higher salaries.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the new normal, we must change how we classify occupations.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This crisis has shown the importance of the work of these essential service workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Only then perhaps, younger Singaporeans will see this as a viable career.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the new normal, we need to change consumers' and service buyers' behaviour where we demand higher standards of procurement practices.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is important that every socially responsible service buyer leads by example and reject service providers that provide services at low cost but always at the expense of the welfare of these essential service workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This crisis has also forced us to reflect our core values and principles to fellow human beings and highlighted our unseen class system.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the same time, it also showed that we can rise to the occasion to put things right.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the new normal, we must change how we regard the migrant workers and welcome them in our community.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must realise that they are the ones who keep Singapore going; cleaners and maintenance workers who keep our neighbourhoods clean and hygienic, workers who keep our transport running so we can get our essential supplies, workers who keep electricity and water flowing to our homes, and workers who provide other services in our neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some of these migrant workers will be housed in vacated school sites to ensure that the safety and welfare of our migrant workers as they continue working during this crisis.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In my constituency, I am heartened that many of my residents demonstrated understanding for the need to have this arrangement but, what if these temporary dormitories must remain for a much longer period?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Do we then adopt the perverse attitude of resisting them again because we do not want them in our backyard?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I hope the new normal for our foreign friends will see them being accepted as a fellow human being who has the right to enjoy the surrounding that they helped to maintain and build.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I see the changes needed for the new normal will complement our efforts to create better jobs, better wages and better welfare for our workers regardless of collar, age, nationalities and sector.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):  : In our efforts to change to the new normal, it is important that we take cognizance of the challenge faced by workers currently as they can be in financial distress due to the crisis now.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): In conclusion, the road ahead will be a long one, but hard times create strong people.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Every one of us must play our part to create a new normal.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will require a shift in mindset for many, but we must also not lose sight of the opportunities ahead.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: With supply chains being impacted, the transport and logistic sector will also be affected.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: As the General Secretary of the Singapore Port Workers' Union, I too, am worried for my brothers and sisters in the sector.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: As compared to the four sectors worst hit by COVID-19, the impact on the transport and logistics sectors are not as pronounced yet.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: However, workers are concerned that they might soon be the "next in line" as they see telling signs of businesses slowing down, a reduction in overtime and incentive earnings as well as being asked to clear their vocational leave due to the low activities.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: It is not just our local workers who are worried about losing their jobs or having a reduction in their take-home pay; our migrant workers in the transport and logistics sectors are also concerned.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: It is in the time of crisis where we must leverage the existing labour-management relations or LMR in short, to help workers and companies through this challenging period.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: I recall when Malaysia first announced the Movement Control Order, the union and PSA management quickly came together to make arrangements to house our Malaysian counterparts in PSA-operated dormitories.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Issues raised by these members were resolved quickly and amicably.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: When the Singapore Government imposed movement restrictions on workers staying at the dormitories, once again, the union and the management partners moved quickly to ensure that the workers' needs are taken care of.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Union leaders and members volunteered their help to support the management in the distribution of meals and daily essentials to these workers in the dormitories.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Some even stepped up to be safe distancing ambassadors at the dormitories and the workplaces.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: These are just some of my personal experiences of how LMR has come to play an essential role during this challenging period.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Even as Singapore gradually reopens our economy, LMR can continue to play a crucial role to ensure that workers can return to work safely and businesses can continue to operate.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: For companies to resume operations, safe management measures must be put in place to minimise the re-emergence of COVID-19 community cases.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: While it might bring about some inconveniences, we all know that these measures are necessary.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Due to this necessity, NTUC has worked with Ong Teng Cheong Labour Leadership Institute and NTUC LearningHub to facilitate the training of union leaders, management partners and union staff as Safe Management Officers.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Having knowledge of safe management measures, union leaders will then be able to work with their management partners to coordinate and implement these measures on the ground.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Each one of us must do our part in adhering to these measures, and I hope that more companies can come on board and get trained so that businesses can continue to operate safely and workers can work in a safe environment.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Another area that we can leverage LMR is in workers’ training.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Compared to pre-COVID times, business activity might not be as high during this period, and we should make use of this time to retrain workers.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: In the port sector, our unions are working with the company to train workers to have dual skills so that they can be cross-deployed across roles.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: One example is how we are encouraging our crane operators and drivers to be reskilled as reefer and equipment maintenance technicians.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: This will not only give the company the flexibility to deploy these workers but also increase the value-add the workers bring to the company.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: I believe we can also explore similar cross-training opportunities in other sectors.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Our unions and management must work even more closely during this challenging period to give confidence to our workers.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: In areas, such as workers’ safety and workers’ training, we should take proactive steps to reassure our workers that we are still doing our utmost best to improve their wages, welfare and work prospects.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Moving forward, what else can we do to keep our workers' jobs and livelihoods?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: At a recent dialogue with PSA Group CEO Tan Chong Meng, our union leaders and PSA’s senior management partners, he shared with us four steps which we can take to help the organisation move forward in post-COVID times.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Taking a page out of that, I feel that these steps are very much relevant to us as a nation.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: But the current climate has exacerbated these norms.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Can the scheme be more favourable to workers who are sole breadwinners of their families, as they would be under greater financial pressure compared to dual-income families?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: As a country, we need to be resilient.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses can use this time to relook at work processes and business strategies while workers can review their training needs.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Take this opportunity to reflect and learn from our past experiences and, hopefully, this will bring about new and innovative solutions which we can leverage when the economy recovers.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Let us work together as a country to develop more win-win solutions for both companies and workers to enable us to be more resilient in the face of future adversities.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: If we can take this period to leverage and adopt technology, increase productivity, reduce our reliance on foreign workforce and reskill our workers to take up new jobs, I believe Singapore is well-poised to take advantage of the new opportunities when the global economy recovers.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: These shifts in the supply chain will cause inter-regional trade to slow down but intra-regional trade will likely grow at a faster pace.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: We must support our businesses to venture into these countries and prepare our workforce to work in these regions.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: This calls for reformation, a change in our convictions or perhaps a rewiring of our professional DNA to open up to transformation or reforms.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Within the last six weeks, we have learnt how to work and study from home, shop online, pay via e-payment, entertain and socially interact online.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Online shopping, ordering of food and services via apps, telecommuting and virtual meetings have become the new norm.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: It has changed the way we look at everything, including the way we transform and the speed of transformation.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, I applaud the Government for sustaining the momentum of digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: But can we do more by extending this support to all sectors?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: So, let us not let these efforts go to waste and press ahead with the transformation.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Whether you are a worker, business owner or even just a citizen of Singapore, let us all do our part to support one another through this challenging period.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Let us unite in solidarity as one people, one nation, one Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mr Speaker, the COVID-19 pandemic and the circuit breaker have gotten many of our families to experience first-hand and, more than ever before, the maniacal task of balancing work, household and childcare duties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Of course, this juggling act is nothing new to many women.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: After all, they had and still assumed the bulk of care-giving duties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For many men like myself, we are getting a really close first-row view of the Herculean effort needed to work from home, get through the work calls while participating in home-based learning (HBL), attending to potty calls and getting food on the table.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The circuit breaker is perhaps also called the “Grand Resocialisation of the Working Men”.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It would have been clear to many by now that juggling work and family should never have been just a women's thing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For many of my male friends with young children and had the chance to work from home, this was the golden age of family togetherness.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are mindful that not all families could do that, especially those in essential services and needed at the frontlines.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are fortunate that we get to participate deeper than ever in our children's lives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We learned how they like to be loved.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We learned how to love all over again.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And amidst this strengthened bedrock of family, we discovered working without ostensibly losing productivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We saw how work and family can thrive if only we work together.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In taking on more care-giving duties, we were forced to probe and challenge the fallacies of gendered norms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There might be a sea change in gendered norms creating a wave of gender equality greater than that experienced before.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is an important change that a progressive society must embrace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And we would do well to keep this momentum going.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As we ought not to let a good crisis go to waste, we should not let this revival of family togetherness go to waste.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For a very long time – even now – we have often framed flexible work arrangement (FWA) as a support to care-givers, especially women on maternity or with young children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have framed it such that women needed more support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is still true that they need more support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But that support must be a family-based one, with men strongly leaning in and making that change.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, wherein FWA is unable to apply for essential workers needed in hospitals, a good childcare is critical for those workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For those who can work from home, both parents really need to be around and both of them will need FWA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The post-circuit breaker and COVID-19 workplace will not and must not be the same.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: FWA is, after all, no longer just a mark of a progressive employer but the enabler of a safer workplace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is their way of building resilience within their workforce and, perhaps, also reap savings from reducing city office rentals and lost productivity through commuting.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Such a right was previously denied to workers because companies found it impossible to adjust their business processes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even traditional companies are conducting their work via Zoom.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Employers should have a better idea now of how to successfully operationalise telecommuting and even other types of FWA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: COVID-19 will bring down the last bastion of industrial era workplace practices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As much as it is difficult to look beyond the next few months on how deep this crisis might be, some forward-looking companies are already looking at the scale and structure of their workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is critical to emerging stronger from this crisis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We will need to consider changing the traditional work structure which is incompatible with the modern workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The traditional work structure assumes that there is a spouse at home or a childcare centre that allows that employee to work nine to 12 hours at the shopfloor or office.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The new work structure prioritises care-giving and equips an employee to work away from the office.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: On the other hand, we do acknowledge that not all businesses have the resources to allow for full telecommuting or FWA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can we also consider enhancing this so that we can entrench telecommuting and FWA for the smaller companies?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Also, even though schools and childcare centres are slowly reopening, we need to be prepared for the possibility that we may have to close them again, should a second wave occur.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must explore how childcare or student care can be better provided if the whole family needs to remain at home.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I have heard of some who even provided babysitting services and entertainment over Zoom for slightly older children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The next thing is that the pandemic has also forced us to re-examine breadwinning vs care-giving.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This crisis has shown that we need both to be as important if we want to evolve to a higher form of the workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But what if one of them has another family member that needs care-giving?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And does keeping a family or household going require as much effort as working?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A shorter duration of child or student care service is needed even by the best of homemakers at times.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I hope that we can value unpaid work more accurately and provide greater support to our homemakers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This crisis has illustrated that we need a care-giving infrastructure as much as building tunnels and data networks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This infrastructure should help families to better cope with family care-giving such as balancing the costs of child and elder care-giving.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, with added medical checks and costs of running childcare and eldercare facilities, fees might increase and increase the burden on families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Lastly, as I was hopelessly trying to attend to home-based learning or HBL and work calls as I was this morning, it dawned on me how lucky I was to have my wife to rotate HBL duties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The support for them is even more needed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, I would like to turn our attention to support for younger Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With no end in sight to the spread of COVID-19, most companies have put off hiring if they have not already reduced excess manpower.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For the graduating class of 2020 and some graduates in 2019, job prospects are not rosy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many of them are concerned about getting jobs, let alone getting one of their preferred ones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: One resident even told me that her University internship has been shortened to part-time because the company's workload had reduced drastically.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This would affect her industrial learning and training exposure.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is not surprising that many of our younger Singaporeans are anxious, having to worry about job prospects on top of the need to pay off their student loans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Since the pandemic started, Young NTUC, the youth wing of NTUC, has been actively engaging younger Singaporeans to help them secure jobs, upgrade their skills and build up resilience in the face of this unprecedented crisis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have extended a series of career programmes to provide timely support and career guidance to help fresh graduates and young workers navigate in a post COVID-19 world.
