speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is primarily because new hires have scant bargaining powers and companies have reduced manpower budget during dire times, and pay increases will not jump dramatically post-recession.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We should also consider incentivising companies to convert these into full-time hires and support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even with the additional traineeships, it might not be possible to absorb so many new graduates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For some younger Singaporeans, it might be better to stay in school, further their studies or pick up new skills.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I suggest that we can help to provide subsidies and loans for second diplomas, degrees or masters to give them the option to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Notwithstanding my suggestions on the Fortitude Budget, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.40 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.19 pm until 4.40 pm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Before the year 2020 began, the global economy was already feeling the effects of the US-China trade war.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The world became a totally different place for everyone.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If the projected shrinkage of the national pie materialises, it would be the worst since Singapore’s Independence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Even so, we cannot realistically expect the cushioning to completely counter what COVID-19 has done or will do – hitting both supply and demand at the same time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Neither can all jobs be saved from this tsunami.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: When push comes to shove, and beyond what the very important Jobs Support Scheme (JSS) can do for businesses and to save the jobs for all local workers, what specificaly will happen to the older segment of our workforce?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Over the past weeks, I have had discussions with union leaders and also with employers' representatives over the subject of older workers, in the context of COVID-19 and our economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They shared their views candidly with me and I have put them together and will share some of their views here, and to make some recommendations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We know from experience and studies that older workers are at greater risk of being retrenched than younger workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We also know that when an older worker loses his job, he will take longer than a younger worker of an otherwise similar profile to find new work, and even then, would in all likelihood take a substantial pay cut.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Therefore, the most merciful thing to do for older workers is to minimise the risk of retrenchment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This Senior Employment Credit, which was announced in the Unity Budget, incentivises companies to hire older workers aged 55 and above.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, it is paying for an outcome and every percentage help to companies is helpful towards inventivising employment and employability of workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I believe that if Government is prepared to do so, it will send a strong and visible signal to both employers and older workers that it is resolute in wanting to save jobs for older workers in this difficult time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In the Unity Budget 2020, Government also announced a new Part-time Re-employment Grant, or PTRG, for employers who offer it to re-employed workers aged 62 and above, who request for it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I hope that Government can apply this incentive to a slightly younger age group from age 55 and above, those who would be employed on that basis for the next one year, because this one year is a critical period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I make this call not only to lower the cost of such workers to their employers who respond positively to suchrequest, but also in view of the fact that COVID-19 is especially harsh toward older persons and employers are therefore also worried about how to deploy such workers and manage their safe return to work; they have concerns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We must therefore find ways to incentivise employers to keep such workers hired, whether full-time or part-time, back to work at the workplace or telecommute, rather than to have the employers decide that they will do without them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: No matter how hard we try, I think it is inevitable that some older workers will be displaced as companies take measures to cope and to transform.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is imperative that we find ways to help as many older workers earn income as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If not, they will become structurally unemployed prematurely, and will then have to depend more on their children, who themselves are under pressure, or on general taxes for support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In this regard, I urge our National Jobs Council to pay due attention to job preservation and job creation for older workers as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Circuit-Breaker period has illustrated cross-industry job possibilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Whether it is Professional Conversion Programmes (PCPs) for older PMEs or full-time/part-time/gig jobs in retail, logistics, healthcare, transport, the public sector and others, let us give older workers a fair go at these opportunities as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I recall that when we battled SARS back in 2003, there were a number of big projects that created many thousands of new jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This time round, the Government has also announced moves to create public and private sector jobs and traineeships.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: MTI has also just very recently announced a very good investment pipeline coming into Singapore that will create thousands of jobs as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Aside from opportunities in areas such as healthcare and e-logistics, we should also consider how areas that might be linked to our longer term security, such as urban farming, renewable energy, such areas as well; whether jobs could also be created are this be given due attention and development.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Over the years, through wage reform, many jobs have wages that have become much more performance-based rather than seniority-based.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I urge employers, therefore, in considering how to manage their excess manpower to be fair.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Please do not target older workers as a category.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Labour Movement and tripartite partners will be on the look-out for age-specific and other unfair practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: COVID-19 has also revealed the sudden disruption to manning when segments of workers are stuck elsewhere even when the company is allowed to operate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There is therefore scope for localisation to help companies be more resilient against such sudden supply disruptions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There will be roles that can be done by willing and properly trained and re-trained local workers, including older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Labour Movement will be keen to work with companies on such initiatives through the Company Training Committees (CTCs) and the NTUC Jobs Security Council (JSC), which will now also function in support of our National Jobs Council.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In this regard, the hiring incentive that was introduced as part of the SkillsFuture Mid-Career Support Package (SMCSP) in February's Unity Budget will come in very handy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This should become part and parcel of the basic Workplace Safety and Health, or WSH, specifications, so that Singapore will have a sustainable operating model in this new normal, and we will not just work on the notion or the assumption that COVID-19 is a one-off event and somehow it will go away and neither it nor anything similar will hit us in future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We have to now be ready for all time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: As part of the reopening of the economy after the circuit breaker ends, workers will progressively return to work in some way.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This will give both they, their employers and their customers greater peace of mind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It would also enable those infected to be identified as early as possible and given treatment, and thus limiting transmission, both in the community and at the workplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: While I call for the preservation of jobs for older workers, this does not mean that the way in which these jobs are to be carried out should remain the same.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Unless companies and workers transform job designs and work processes, and increase their use of technology and spur innovation, they will not escape the worst that this storm will bring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This COVID-19 storm is so furious that there simply would not be enough resources to prop up zombie companies and jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This means that we must spur companies to press on with job redesign.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I call for practical support for companies, again, in both monetary and non-monetary, such as expertise terms, to help them quickly redesign jobs and processes that incorporate the following key dimensions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: First, how to re-engineer processes and use technology to render more jobs Easier, Safer and Smarter, or what we call ESS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: ESS jobs, the concept is not new at all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The hon Mr Lim Swee Say, when he was Secretary-General NTUC as well as Manpower Minister, tried very hard to promote the adoption and innovation in this area.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Next, with many SMEs struggling badly and yet in total employing some two-thirds of our workforce, and within that two-thirds, many are older workers as well, how we help SMEs redesign processes, jobs, their entire operations for this new enviornment and transform, if we can do that, that will really move the needle as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is not easy; it has been tried before; it is so dispersed – very hard to do.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But if that ground does not move or does not move quick or well enough, then actually it is very difficult to move the overall; it is just simply because the number of businesses that are SMEs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Again, tapping into the moment that we are in now, where everybody knows that we have to change, not because you like it but because that is the reality, then let us do it with a concerted tripartite effort, at least minimally, let us target the more promising SMEs, and through them to show to the rest, let them lead the pack in this transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This topic has been covered in depth earlier by the Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon, so I will not belabour the points on training except to make one, which is once again call on employers to remember and to please invest in the training and re-training of your older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Do not leave them out, do not just do it for your younger workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: An employer who views his older workers as assets and another employer who views them as liabilities will both be right, because they will each act in a self-fulfilling manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is the best favour we can do for ourselves in this environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This capacity to face up to situations, however intractable, however unpleasant, is one of the great qualities for survival.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: A people able to look facts squarely in the face, able to calculate the odds, to weigh the chances and then to decide to go for it, are a people not likely to go under." Mr Deputy Speaker, we are that people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Even as we Singaporeans slowly return to work, we must be mindful that many of our migrant worker friends cannot.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They remain restricted to their dormitories to help protect our community from infection risks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Initial shortcomings aside, we are now sparing no effort to make things right.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has committed to improve living conditions for migrant workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But this only addresses the public health aspects of our migrant worker population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are more fundamental questions about the structure of our economy and our reliance on foreign labour that must be explored if we are to emerge stronger from this pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Old assumptions about these matters have never been properly examined.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What are the reasons behind this vast increase in foreign labour and what have been the effects on our economy?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The facts are that successful cities throughout history have grown rapidly through migration and not because of the fertility of the existing population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If we had remained part of Malaysia, we would have grown through domestic migration from the hinterland.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The major Chinese cities have grown through domestic migration, as has Jakarta, Tokyo, London, New York.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Because we have no hinterland, every migrant is, by definition, foreign.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But like those global cities, we attract migrants because we offer the opportunity to build a better life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, migration is still a policy choice, even within a country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Chinese cities impose the Hukou system, which differentiates between urban residents and rural migrants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Malaysians cannot freely migrate between Peninsular and East Malaysia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, the question of whether to slow or stop migration is relevant even when migrants carry the same passport.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, when can we justify growing the labour force through migration?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We permit migration to grow our economy faster than our purely local labour force can.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This gives us a bigger pie so that everyone – migrants and locals alike – can meet their needs and aspirations better.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But even if overall growth is positive, migration creates winners and losers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We have an obligation to the public to understand how labour migration affects Singaporean jobs and to discuss the consequences of migration on our economy – positive and negative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Some argue that reliance on low cost work permit holders has made our construction industry less skill intensive than other developed countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There is some evidence for that, but that is not the whole story.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Within the 20% of construction workforce who are locals, more than half are actually PMETs – our project and engineering managers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In comparison, in the United States, one in four of their construction workforce are PMETs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, because less skilled positions are filled by migrant workers, the Singaporean workforce can actually be more skill intensive compared to their counterparts elsewhere.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are also benefits to Singaporeans in manual construction work as they supervise migrant workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Median wages for Singaporean supervisors and foremen are close to $3,000 a month – much higher than similarly skilled workers in some other sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Migrant workers may well complement our Singaporean core in construction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, we must also consider cases where migrant labour may have mixed effects on Singaporean workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In food and beverage (F&B) services, and cleaning and landscape maintenance, the share of foreign labour is also high.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: At the broad sectoral level, about half of the workers are foreign.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the wages and conditions of work for locals are not as good as in construction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We should ask whether this is because migrant labour in these sectors often fill the same types of jobs that locals do, including supervisor positions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is the degree of substitutability that matters and migrant labour in many service sectors could potentially replace local labour, which would then pressure wages and benefits downwards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Taking a step back, the next question is how our migrant labour policy affects our economic structure, productivity and growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The economist Alwyn Young famously argued in 1992 that Singapore's rapid growth was driven by the accumulation of labour and capital rather than by total factor productivity growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporean economists Linda Lim and Pang Eng Fong, in an article published on academia.sg on 2 June, noted that concerns on the impact of foreign labour date back to the 1970s.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They hold the view that "an over-reliance on cheap foreign labour...distorts factor prices and resource allocation, resulting in economic inefficiency and inequality, without enabling higher growth." These are, as you can see, very old questions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, we seem to have made little progress in understanding the role of foreign labour in Singapore's economy since then.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are relatively few rigorous pieces of research on the Singapore economy and labour market, despite the high quality of our economists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is partially because microeconomic data on the Singapore labour market is rarely available to researchers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It does not need to be this way.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Malaysian government commissioned the report and provided detailed labour market data.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What would we find in Singapore if we were to conduct such a study?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the quality of the public discourse is harmed when such research is not put into the public eye, is not taught or conducted by our Universities and is not debated by the public.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is an issue that goes beyond politics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is part of the democratic discourse that we need to progress as a nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A great society is able to confront the unpleasant realities beneath the surface and resolve to make painful but necessary changes for collective progress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our present economic structure and migrant labour system has created entrenched interests who would be harmed by and will resist any attempts at reform.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I speak not just of the obvious interests among business owners who rely on migrant workers but also of each one of us as ordinary Singaporeans who benefit from the system regardless whether we directly employ a migrant worker.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The high quality of life that we take for granted is built in part on the ceaseless toil of a vast trickle-up economy of hundreds of thousands of migrant workers, Malaysian day workers and even our own Singaporean low-wage workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We must examine the hidden costs to social stability when we expect to have a first-world standard of living, delivered at third-world prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Despite what we consider to be low wages and difficult working conditions, many migrant workers want to work in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They build a pathway to the middle class or better back home with their earnings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our own low-wage workers do and must continue to get substantial Government support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But while we do not bear the moral stain of forced labour, we have fallen short of providing dignified work conditions for all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our collective indifference to the struggles of low-wage workers in Singapore, whatever their nationality, has hurt our ability to cope with this crisis and it will continue to harm our ability to build a compassionate and resilient society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If we fail to build the capacity to question, understand and reform our system, if necessary, to provide better treatment and living wages for low-wage workers, we will each bear the complicity of the bystander.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We will face the question in the coming months of how to restructure our economy and society for a more sustainable and resilient future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But we must resist the temptation to use the reserves simply to preserve the economic model of the past in the hopes that we can return to it once the COVID-19 outbreak subsides.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Is the right economic model for our future that which has driven us over the past decades, one where we aim as far as possible to have Singaporeans take up PMET jobs and migrant workers the rest?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think there are some real difficulties with that approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is akin to running an army with only sergeants and officers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If we recognise that all work, especially socially essential work, has value, then we need to agree there is no shame in having Singaporeans take up manual and service jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The only shame is if we who have power and influence fail to ensure that the conditions of work and wages in these service jobs are such that Singaporeans find no dignity in taking them up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: More generally, we should realise now that it is neither safe nor resilient to decouple essential service jobs that must physically take place in Singapore from residency in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is not a problem unique to Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The unseen engine behind global cities worldwide is a vast army of essential workers who are frequently paid too little to live next to those they provide services to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has been able to cope in part because migrant workers and Malaysian day workers are willing to do these jobs at wages which are nearly unliveable in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But it is not sustainable to depend on continuing low wages in migrant worker source countries to excuse us from finding a solution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If anything, we should recognise that essential services and manual jobs, by their physical presence requirements, offer some resilience against a world where office work can be shifted globally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Working from home has weakened the physical link between doing business in Singapore and having that business actually be done by a Singaporean here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Rather than develop an economy where most Singaporeans, despite their different skills and talents, feel compelled to earn degrees to hold down PMET jobs, we can build an economy that also includes many skilled and decently paid craftsmen, technicians and service workers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With COVID-19, nobody really knows when things will start to brighten up.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But we can take heart that our Government is determined to make things right.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Businesses and individuals must make the best use of resources provided by our Government and put our best foot forward.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is heartwarming to hear about the businesses who returned the benefits from the Jobs Support Scheme (JSS) to the Government.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Then, there are others, some food and beverage businesses, who are cooking and distributing food to the needy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And those who helped free up commercial resources for mass production of surgical masks or pooling together resources to sew reusable masks.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many of my residents and supporters donated masks, face shields, sanitisers and vitamins, and some of them even donated their $600 which they received from the Government.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is truly a display of our nation's fortitude.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But in the meantime, some challenges remain which require attention.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: First, more help for home-grown large companies with a localised workforce which have ventured abroad.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The focus of our four Budgets is to preserve lives and livelihoods, saving and creating jobs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They hire many Singaporeans; they venture and expand overseas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Now that the global economy is doing poorly, they are also struggling to keep above water.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It takes decades for some of these made-in-Singapore brands to achieve the regional and global recognition.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad that Temasek came in to help SIA so that we do not lose our national carrier.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like to talk about the construction sector.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Before I proceed further, I would like to declare my interest as a professional engineer (PE) and my involvement in property development and construction.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At first, when the Government announced that the construction sector can start work in Phase One, all the contractors were very happy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: All those businesses who can start business in Phase One, they were very happy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But their happiness turned to frustration soon when they found out about the number of approvals required before they can start work.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And I have received many complaints from them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They are faced with many challenges and let me share with the House.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, all the current dormitories do not comply.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, if you do not have dormitories that comply, no approval for safe dormitories, cannot start work.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, how to comply to new requirements within a short period?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Normally, such requirements, the process of approval from various Government agencies will take at least three months.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Medical experts have been saying that as long as people live together, they are likely to infect each other since COVID-19 is very contagious.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, is the 6 m2 requirement much safer than the current provision?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For those who are currently stay in factory-converted dormitories (FCD) or in the construction temporary quarters (CTQ) where all their workers are healthy, can we let them maintain the status quo for now, quickly arrange swab tests for the workers so that they can start work without shifting them and without further delay?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Now, every contractor is scratching their head – how to meet the new MOM requirements?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can MOM be more flexible on the existing CTQ and FCD?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The next challenge is the compulsory swab tests.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why those S Pass holders who are not living in dormitory are unable to register for swab tests?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Those who are housed in their own factory dormitory, well taken care of for the last two months, just because they are not swab tested, they cannot start work.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A contractor said: 等来等去, swab 来, swab 去, 天都亮了。 This compulsory swab test exercise can easily stretch until August or September.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The next challenge – compulsory safe management officer (SMO), safe distancing officer (SDO).

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For contractors to start work, they must have SMO, SDO.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There is long queue too for training of SMO and SDO.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why this is not conducted during circuit breaker?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can we have more sessions so that this does not become a bottleneck?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, no SMO, no SDO, no start work.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Suddenly, I received many text messages and phone calls.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Contractors have to give consent to MOM to deploy their workers who have recovered from COVID-19.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why does not MOM just return the workers to the rightful employers?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why force people to give up their workers?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For some sub-contractors, they said they only have two or three charge hands, that means, important staff.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And they say if MOM were to take them away, they cannot function when their works can restart.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For those who are forced to take in workers, also not happy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They said it is very difficult to use other people's workers to work in your team.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, it works only for housekeeping or general works.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, why not leave it to them to handle their own workers?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This pandemic further illustrates the need to have multi-agencies working together and not in silos.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: BCA, MOM, MOH and FAST Team all are working very hard but they need to work together, and also get industry input and not force their way through.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There needs to be more communication so that the intent is well understood.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many contractors I spoke to say let those workers who are healthy and swab tested, start work first.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, what they want is let more projects start but gradually.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For those who do not have enough workers to start, contractors will know how to work out among themselves.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With all these challenges, many will not be able to start work for at least another three months, perhaps September.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And the income will only come in another two to three months later, maybe end of the year.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Operating costs are going up due to more stringent requirements while productivity is going down.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am afraid many firms will go bust.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As one contractor puts it: all these administrative roadblocks are turning Phase One restart into an extended circuit breaker for the construction industry.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I wish to appeal for more support for the construction industry.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But contractors have many other bills to pay, such as machineries rental, dormitory, loans and so on.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They have been having zero income since April.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Because currently, the swab test is free only up to August.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But after August, every worker needs to be sent for a swab test every 14 days and they did not price in all these costs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Or perhaps by then, we can remove the swab test.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, they are given 100% waiver for June only.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, can we give them full rebate until August?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Third, the industry feedback is that it seems like there is not much help given by JTC.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Fourth, another group of people serving the construction industry – that is, consultants, engineers and architects – will they be given similar support like what we have given to contractors, especially the JSS, because they are very worried about the staff cost?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will resident engineers and resident technical officers be similarly supported?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Because in the industry, they are very confused – they are not sure.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: My next topic in this speech is the opening of sports facilities.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have always been a huge advocate of active living.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With this pandemic, sport has taken a huge hit.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A resident, Josephine, told me that she had vertigo 20 years ago and it went away because of sport.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With the circuit breaker, her vertigo came back with a vengeance.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I urge the Government to consider allowing the commencement of non-contact sports during Phase One.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A study was done by the Italian Ministry of Sport and Italian Olympic Committee to evaluate the risk of contracting COVID-19 for various sports.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The risk was found to be non-existent or weak for individual non-contact sports like athletics, that means running, sailing, open water swimming, golf and tennis.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, many other countries allowed some sports in their first phase of restart with some safety measures.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For example, Malaysia allows two golfers per flight, but cannot share buggy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Swimmers are back in the pools in Australia, the Netherlands, Japan, China and so on with safe distancing measures, such as one swimmer per lane and some started without the opening of changing rooms.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can we not open up our stadiums with SafeEntry, crowd size control, designated lane usage and so on?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure it can be much safer than some of the park connectors which are so congested.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, many associations such as Singapore Swimming Association, many clubs already have thought about this.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They would like more guidance and to resume their activities.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Government work with SportsSG to determine the sports suitable to make a return for Phase One with relevant safety guidelines?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And I hope whatever measures that we want to put in place, the training can commence now.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Otherwise, it may lead to bottlenecks like what happened to the construction industry.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So many people feel so stressed when they cannot do their favourite sports.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Also, there are many freelance coaches who can no longer survive without income.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):  : Some residents told me that this Fortitude Budget gave more support to businesses, but less to families.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The increased utilities expenses due to telecommuting may have exceeded the $100 subsidy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They hope that people living in 3-room flats can also receive grocery vouchers, if their per capita income is relatively low.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The outbreak has also quickened the pace of digitalisation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, many people are worried that the vulnerable groups may not be able to keep up with this pace.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government can continue to pay attention to those who cannot afford a computer or data connection, and make sure that those students whose family environment is not conducive for home-based learning are not lagging further behind.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, while we introduce e-payment in the neighbourhood, the seniors should not feel that they cannot adapt.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: We must also look after the physical and mental well-being of our people.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Singapore has pulled through many crises in the past.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Each time, we have not just survived, but emerged stronger.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: This time let us again pull together and help every Singaporean get through this.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just as gold is refined in fire so also do the testing and hardships of life build character.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today we are debating the Fortitude Budget – a Budget to strengthen Singapore as we forge ahead.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In light of the heightened concern on being retrenched or terminated, it is important that our workers have sufficient protection from disguised retrenchments, which would not only remove any retrenchment benefit that a worker may be entitled to and would desperately need in today’s job climate, but would also obscure our ability to monitor the situation on retrenchments.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How soon is “some time soon” and how will employees who have been terminated know whether or not there are any plans to fill the vacancy any time soon?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As employees need to bring a claim of wrongful dismissal to the Tripartite Alliance of Dispute Management within one month of being terminated, the uncertainty and practical difficulties of this guideline could have a real impact on the employee’s ability to potentially seek redress.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here I would like to make the point that with the accelerated digitalisation of the world, the skill gap needed to be overcome by job seekers has, in some instances, also increased tremendously.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If not, the gap dividing the people who have the ability to understand the digital world and the equipment and those who do not, that gap will exponentially widen.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Is the current training support sufficient, especially for those who require extensive reskilling of workers after their jobs may become obsolete in the post COVID world, especially where digitalisation is concerned?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While there is only so much that can be done to create jobs, would the Government consider promoting mentorship programmes as well, where the focus is on professional development and exposure, though may not necessarily be salaried or fully salaried.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Being able to work on ad hoc projects, for instance, to be provided guidance from an industry professional on what courses are industry relevant, as well as being introduced to a network of other professionals may also be invaluable for job seekers even if they are unable to find a permanent job at the moment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: COVID-19 has accelerated digitalisation, making digital literacy something necessary; no longer merely supplementary.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The global mass working from home exercise has caused employers to rethink the need for employees to be physically present in the workplace, with some companies like Facebook even thinking of hiring remote staff who would permanently telecommute.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What I am getting at is that COVID-19 has changed the labour market, the need for such large commercial rental space and also skillsets.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The strong uptake of digitalisation and support for telecommuting will provide opportunities job seekers in previous generations would find hard to imagine.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, while it may be that job seekers will face global competition, the converse is also true – job seekers have opportunities from all around the world, able to live in Singapore but able to work for an overseas employer.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Riding this wave of digitalisation is therefore key to ensuring our Singaporeans are equipped and ready for borderless job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For others, the greater support for working from home, that is, flexible work arrangements, may mean greater opportunities for mothers seeking to re-enter the workforce.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We can convert adversity into strength, supporting workers and businesses in digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Companies who can implement work from home arrangements well, will in turn be able to reduce the commercial floor space they need, reducing rental fees and overhead charges.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would free up costs in the long run to invest in the development of personnel, it will also allow more money to be deployed into planning for the future instead of paying large amounts of commercial rent; it will allow effective utilisation of technology; it will create a future for the company through virtual communication.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How companies cope and adapt to the COVID-19 virus is important to the Fortitude Budget.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And at this point, I like to record my thanks to the Deputy Prime Minister and his MOF team for putting out a fourth Budget in record time.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, the Job Support Scheme focuses on the ability to captalise on our reserves to support employers at this time.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is good that the sectors of aviation and aerospace, tourism, hospitality, conventions and exhibitions and the built environment will receive 1st tier support for June to August 2020.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even for essential projects that have been allowed to reopen, many have not been able to.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, many will not be able to hit the ground running at pre-circuit breaker levels even if they can reopen in Phase One.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides getting workers swabbed, having dormitories cleared, those in some industries may need to seek workers from other companies due to border restrictions and manpower supply shortages.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Those with many workers who are still in Malaysia will have to plan their teams without the level of manpower that they once had.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even for those who have been able to work from home, their clients or customers may not have sufficient cash flow to pay them for the services rendered during the circuit breaker period owing to the whole demand-supply shock and disruption.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a result of the circuit breaker, home renovation works had to be halted.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some families had to rent another place for accommodation for an extended period of time and now need to rethink whether they need to extend their tenancies and pay additional rent because their home is still in the middle of a renovation that has been halted.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Other families have or are still roughing it out in their half-completed homes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The home renovation sector is part of the built environment sector that requires specific approval to resume works.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are still difficulties that some home renovation contractors face.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I understand that testing of workers is essential.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will seriously assist the family waiting for their renovation to be completed in their actual home, the contractor as well as the sub-contractors.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Something important that arises out of the COVID-19 pandemic and our response to it, is ensuring social inclusion in a society of increased digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is good that there will be Digital Ambassadors who will help introduce stallholders and the elderly to the online world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is something that needs to be watched out for and bridged, where possible, ensuring that individuals and families can have access to wifi and certain core digital equipment that may be deemed essential in this day and age.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I look forward to hearing the details on how this will be addressed nationally.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the meantime, we will continue to carry out the local laptop, wifi and free Zoom tuition programmes in Ulu Pandan, the constituency I serve and I am responsible for.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In concluding, Sir, I wish to lean on the wise words of an Ulu Pandan Pioneer Generation resident whom I briefly met at a mask collection point over the last weekend.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He shared with me a formula to overcome this crisis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He said, and I quote: "We must have the right stamina We must have the right attitude For we are all sons of the soil." Indeed, he is right.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are all in this together – facing this crisis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the right stamina, with the right attitude and with the right unity, we will prevail.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):  : This is the fourth budget tabled in this House in the span of a few months.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I have submitted several proposals and expressed concern in my speech for the previous Budget debate and I will state a few more suggestions and would also like to seek some clarification in my speech this time.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In recent months, I have been contacted by some of my residents who are asking for exemption in their rental fees during these challenging times.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Any support in this matter can further ease the burden of Singaporeans living in rental flats under the HDB Public Rental Scheme.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Such assistance will help them to maintain a financial position, which is already weak to begin with, from becoming fragile.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is especially for those who are striving to strengthen their financial position in order to get their permanent dream home.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The second issue is also related to the provision of support for low-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Currently, our country is undertaking government-led efforts to spur our society towards digitalisation to achieve the goal of a "Smart Nation".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I am confident that we want every Singaporean regardless of their socio-economic background to move together and not be left behind in this digitalisation effort.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has further highlighted the importance for every home to have an internet connection to enable learning and to work from home.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe many members of this Chamber have met low-income residents who sought help to appeal on their behalf about their outstanding internet subscription bills.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: At this time, I think it is not wrong to say that internet connectivity is a basic need.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Presently, there is a government rebate scheme to help ease the cost of basic necessities such as the utilities rebate, and the services and conservancy charges (S&CC) rebate.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I sincerely hope that both of my proposals will be given the best consideration.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The next matter is the COVID-19 swab test.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It has been reported that all teachers and staff of pre-school centres and kindergartens have to undergo the COVID-19 swab test.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As explained by the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) through media reports, this is a precautionary measure in preparation for the reopening of kindergartens and pre-school centres.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For the use of reserves, the process to go through is that the government needs to provide a detailed explanation that is supported by information and facts to the President.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The President will consult and consider with assistance and advice from the Council of Presidential Advisers (CPA) whether to approve the government's request or otherwise.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Elected President scheme was introduced in 1991.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: One of the main objectives of the scheme was for the elected President, who received the the people’s mandate through the electoral process, to be given the role or responsibility as the co-protector or the second key to the national reserves.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In short, the elected President has the power to say "yes" or "no" if the Government wants to use the national reserves.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of you may remember the title of the song as being "Too Much, Too Little, Too Late".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Incidentally, this past Tuesday marked 18 weeks since the first confirmed case of COVID-19 in Singapore on 23 January 2020.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For a song, 18 weeks is a good run on the billboard.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For us in Singapore, these have been 18 very long and extraordinary weeks.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Here in Parliament, we have also witnessed unprecedented times.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But there have been varied reactions to our commitment, much like the title of the song.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A small number say: "Too much for them, too little for me, too late for us." One example is the Jobs Support Scheme (JSS).

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some say that "you have given too much to MNCs, they are profitable at the end of the day, give less to them, because there’s too little for me.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And even if you do, it may be too late for us." Is it really true?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That more for them means less for us and therefore, less for them means more for us?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To me, it is a misinterpretation of the intent.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is not "for them", the MNCs, but for "us", the jobs that they provide.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are preserving the jobs, the jobs that could easily go somewhere else at a moment's notice.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is an investment, an investment for jobs, for jobs to remain here.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But the MNCs know that here in Singapore, we care for our workers, we care enough to pay a significant part of their salary, so that in the future, the company, the MNCs remain and thus, the jobs also remain.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are not in a dichotomy of one or the other, all livelihoods that we can preserve, secure, retain are worth the investment in.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And we cannot wait until it is too late to do so.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On the other hand, for the COVID-19 Support Grant (CSG) or SIRS for self-employed people, these are unprecedented as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A serious commitment of this Government to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Worried about our health, also about money, worried about how we are using our reserves.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some say that this is too much, too generous.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Others say it is too little left for the future or too late to reverse the positions that have already been made.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, there are also others who say that there is too much in the reserves.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is too little that is being spent on us and it is too late to make a difference.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But, it can never be too much to do whatever we can to save lives, to save jobs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We cannot, in the biggest existential crisis that we are facing since the withdrawal of the British in 1967, to do too little too late.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, that the decision on maintaining our reserves has been the right one.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can be comforted that it was not wrong.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even if some believe that we have too much reserves, it is not wrong too, to use whatever we have to save lives and save jobs, to not use too little during this crisis and that we did not wait till it was too late for us to do so.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is also not wrong to ensure that the keys to our reserves ensure that we use it prudently, wisely, rightly.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the same song, the lyrics in the rift say, "Somewhere we lost the key, So little left for you and me and it's clear to see." We have a responsible Government and we have a second key – in the hand of our elected President.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In taking prudent decisions, we are able to save wisely, spend prudently and put it to the best use possible.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are still others who talk about other issues that have arisen during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, migrant workers have been a hot topic for a number of weeks.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some say that too much is being done for migrant workers, too little for the rest of us, too late in reacting to the high numbers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Still more also say: too much talk over the years, too little done in the past, too late to try again.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even more may exclaim: too much reliance on foreign workers, too little investment in our local workforce, too late now for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Is it really too much, too little or too late?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can all admit that we can do much more to improve living conditions but we are certainly not housing our migrant workers in slums.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can all admit that we must not pay too little attention to building up local capability, especially in construction in our built sector, but there are certainly sacrifices that we must all make.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But there is one point worth clarifying on the accusation of being too late, that we did too much in tracing and testing, resulting in too much an increase in numbers; that we did too little, resulting in high daily numbers for our migrant workers; that it was too late, resulting in the explosion of numbers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am not medically trained, but I believe that the transparency of our system in identifying every risk – isolating and putting the workers in quarantine – is far better than classifying some while ignoring others, just so that our numbers may look better.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some expound conspiracy theories, saying that it is a mess in the facilities, that is why there are so many cases.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Again, I am not a medical professional, but I believe cases do not just burn themselves out.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is not just a medical 21 days of being in isolation and, therefore, there are no other cases.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At home, let us say, you have a family of five people.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It does not mean that all four other family members get the common cold instantly.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Maybe your wife will get it the next day.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And maybe your kid did not catch it from you but caught it from your wife, not you.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, it is not as simple as saying 21 days have passed, something must be horrendously wrong and, therefore, we have so many cases.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But what we must know is that we must never be afraid that just because we do so many tests, resulting in too high a number, because, as I have mentioned earlier, it is far better for us to be transparent, cautious and safe than to regret later and say, really, it was too late.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If not, we will really be accused of doing too little, too late.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are all in the same choppy oceans now but, perhaps, we are all in different vessels.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is not just about having a great captain on every boat or lighthouse to provide comfort.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We need the coast guard, lighter boatmen, pilots, pilot boats to help the different vessels.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have different needs and are in different situations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If not, even if we spend too much, it will truly be too little for some and too late for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The chorus of the song goes, "Too much, too little, too late to ever try again.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Too much, too little, too late, we knew it had to end." It is a nice sentimental chorus for a song, but it will be a tragedy if we ever have to sing about this, about our Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The central focus of the Fortitude Budget is on jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In the COVID-19 environment, many businesses face uncertainty about the future and many are scaling down their hiring as they worry about an impending recession.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many businesses ask, "With a slowing economy, would my business be able to survive, much less employ new staff?" Thus, the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package would help to assure jobseekers, especially those entering the workforce after graduation, that there are still job opportunities and skills training or upgrading available to citizens who want a job.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It has been seven weeks since the Solidarity Budget was announced.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Over the past two months, due to the circuit breaker measures, many businesses which are non-essential have to cease operations totally.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Even if the homes are not owned by them but rented by them, or even if they are staying with their parents, they would not be eligible if the annual values of the home exceed $21,000.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I received many messages from self-employed persons like housing agents, insurance agents, tuition teachers, instructors, contractors and people in the sales industry.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They said that for the last two months, their income had fallen drastically because they were all required to stay at home and unable to carry out their business activities.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For some of the housing agents, they said their income had been totally zero for the past two months, even though they tried to sell properties online.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They dread that their income will remain zero for the third month because the Council of Estate Agents had informed them that they are still not allowed to bring their clients to the show flats.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many of them accept that it is part of their duty as Singaporeans to stay at home and are willing to do their part to break the COVID-19 virus transmission.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, for a person who has a net trade income of, say, $120,000 per annum or an average of $10,000 per month, he would not be eligible for the income relief scheme.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: From earning an average of $10,000 per month, he now gets zero income for two or even three months.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Hence, he would struggle to bear the entire expenses for his family.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I have received emails from my residents appealing for help.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: One said that she is a licensed estate agent divorced a few years ago.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: She has four children aged between 10 and 15 in her custody.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: She has a wheelchair-bound mother to look after.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Another wrote to me stating that she needed to financially provide for her aged parents and their children.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And on top of all their daily living expenses, they still had to pay for their housing mortgage loans for the past two months.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The recent announcement that some of their businesses cannot resume even after 2 June has caused them more financial pain as they have to struggle for another one to two months.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But I submit that the fact that some self-employed persons who had a higher income in the last year or that they lived in a home with a higher annual value of more than $21,000 does not mean that they have the ability to survive two to three more months without any income.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It all depends on their savings and expenses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In a recent OCBC survey of Singaporeans' ability to save, 18% of working adults say that they do not have savings to last them one month, and 28% say that they do not have savings to last them beyond three months.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: That means that 46% cannot last three months.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, if these self-employed persons had less savings or they had higher expenses, should they be left without any support from the Government?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If they happen to stay with their parents in a better home, should they also be excluded from the Self-Employed Persons Income Relief Scheme?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If the intent of the Government is to protect the livelihood of the workers, then I submit that we must do more to help self-employed persons who are badly affected by the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Even as we ask our citizens to make a sacrifice, the Government should also bear part of the sacrifice with them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The $1,000 per month for nine months is not a big sum of money, compared to what they have lost during this period.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This group of people are not asking for charity.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They would be much happier carrying out their commercial activities, earning their income based on their skills and expertise.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They do expect a drastic fall in their income due to the expected financial downturn even after the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But what they are asking for is some form of financial support to tide them over to meet their basic expenses during this period because their businesses are forced to cease operations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am of the view that this request is not unreasonable.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Since the last quarter of 2019 before COVID-19 hit, I had described Singapore's job market as experiencing "persistent showers with pockets of sunshine".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With the evolving COVID-19 situation, the weather has become even more uneven and unpredictable.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, unlike cyclical downturns, with COVID-19, there is much less visibility about the future.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is hard to tell if a bigger storm is brewing or how long it may last.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Bad weather is something my husband and I learnt to embrace.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On our travels, we like to go hiking.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When we were younger, we used to fret whenever the weather turned bad.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Later, we learnt a saying that is popular among Scandinavians, that "there is no such thing as bad weather, only unsuitable clothing." Even with the best of plans, bad weather cannot always be avoided.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Instead of being frustrated, we learnt to gear up and be ready to step out in any weather.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is not just to wander aimlessly, but to try and make our way to where there are clearer skies and to get back in the sun.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It takes a lot of effort, but it is better than to be stuck with nowhere to go.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: That is how I think we can deal with the situation today.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Focus on getting ready for a possible storm, and put all our energies into gearing up.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Part of the gearing up is the Jobs Support Scheme (JSS) and other support programmes under the Unity, Resilience, Solidarity and Fortitude Budgets.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Each of these schemes is helping to cushion the impact of the COVID-19 outbreak on the labour market.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They are providing much needed cover to businesses and workers, saving jobs and livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If we did not have this cover, we would already be drenched in soaring unemployment, as can be seen in some countries.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We would be dealing with a very different problem today.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We must gear up for further job losses, although we do not know exactly how severe it will be.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Uncertainty about the future will also moderate hiring.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Besides defending existing jobs, we must try to open up many more pathways to jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It reminds us to plan ahead before the storm hits.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will be critical in the months ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There will have to be a big push for many pathways to jobs: pathways for retrenched and mid-career persons from all sectors and all ages, middle-aged or older; pathways for fresh graduates from our ITEs, Polytechnics, Universities and other educational institutions; pathways for self-employed persons (SEPs) who want to remain SEPs or to move into regular employment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will need tight coordination to create multiple pathways for a whole range of workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But in today’s context, it may not be an immediate job or even a permanent one at the start.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It should, however, be a pathway that allows for people to use their time meaningfully, learn something useful and gain valuable experience.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As much as possible, it should be a path to a better, brighter future.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have a real stake in doing this well.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Not only do we want to enable every Singaporean to remain meaningfully occupied, we want to help each citizen to preserve his or her human capital and to build on it.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Collectively for Singapore, this means not allowing the downturn to erode our human capital but, instead, to enhance it so that we can emerge stronger as one.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is the challenge we should set for ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I need not tell Members how enormous this challenge is.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Each of these 29,000, on average, already involves painstaking work.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In many cases, there are job and skills mismatches.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In others, there are mismatches of wage expectations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In today’s context, we must add another significant mismatch and it has to do with timing.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
