text: Many jobseekers will be hungry for work and school leavers eager to start their careers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But employers will be hesitant and not ready to hire.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: After all, they may not themselves have enough visibility about the business.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a result, there will likely be many more jobseekers than jobs available.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We must expect many roadblocks on previously well-established pathways to jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a millennial might put it, it is an epic challenge to create new pathways for 100,000 people under such circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The target of close to 100,000 opportunities is not insurmountable but the NJC will have to work very, very hard to create the pathways, involving multiple partners.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Notwithstanding the challenges, our top-most priority is still to promote jobs and making sure that jobseekers have access to them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many of the permanent positions in the public sector are a result of hiring plans being brought forward.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These include science and engineering roles in agencies like HTX and positions in early childhood education, healthcare and long-term care.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also ramp up capacity of career conversion programmes to help jobseekers reskill for new roles in the private sector, such as for Auxiliary Police Officers in the security sector.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will work with employers to prepare them for redeployment rather than unemployment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In this climate, I think we should be realistic but also opportunistic – in a good way.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Employers may hold back job offers but we can encourage them to offer traineeship or attachment pathways, through meaningful funding support.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These traineeships may not provide the same security as a job, but they will provide valuable industry-relevant experience and better position a jobseeker when the economy recovers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One example is familiar to us – Carousell, a homegrown tech scale-up – no longer a start-up but a scale-up.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Carousell created a new trainee position for graduates to learn how the company strategises to grow its markets and build customer loyalty.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The experience of working in a start-up culture or scale-up culture is certainly useful.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are also very keen to open up attachment pathways for mid-career jobseekers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the first NJC meeting yesterday, there was intense discussion about the potential for such experienced mid-career persons to help businesses transform, particularly SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will supplement the resources of hard-pressed SMEs to build up their capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: More pathways of this type could be win-win.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Another important pathway could be through the Continuing Education and Training (CET) Centres and Institutes of Higher Learning.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While looking to land a job or attachment pathway, it is useful to acquire new skills through a structured programme.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Such programmes can have a combination of classroom training and company involvement, such as industrial project work.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To help jobseekers find the most suitable pathway, we will expand our ground presence.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We now have five career centres island-wide and partnerships with NTUC’s e2i, the Social Service Offices, CDCs, self-help groups, such as MENDAKI.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To be closer to jobseekers, we aim to build up a presence in all HDB towns through satellite career centres.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But in any case, not every jobseeker needs to come through WSG's physical door.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is why we have significantly built up our digital presence and range of digital services on MyCareersFuture.sg.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Even before the circuit breaker, we rolled out a series of thematic Virtual Career Fairs (VCFs) in sectors, such as ICT, Logistics & Transport, and Healthcare and Community Care.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will bring this to the SGUnited Traineeships as well.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will spare no effort to open up new pathways for jobseekers and guide them appropriately – as big a push as we can muster.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But for matches to happen, I urge jobseekers to keep an open mind – stay open to pathways that you would not have considered previously.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Give the employers a chance and give yourself a chance.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To extend our reach to more workers and employers, we have been working closely with our tripartite partners, with encouraging results.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When air travel came to a standstill due to COVID-19, NTUC played an instrumental role in kick-starting job redesign projects.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: NTUC's e2i has been working through the NTUC Job Security Council to push out short-term and long-term job opportunities for retrenched workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will reach out and partner more trade associations and chambers to open up pathways in their respective sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We value the networks that they have and we believe that by working closely with them, we will be able to reach more businesses and enable more pathways to open up for jobseekers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I want to also add that these partnerships can include SEP associations like those for sports coaches and media freelancers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This may sound frightening and, indeed, we should not underestimate how rough the weather might become.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But we are not going in without some cover.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In fact, I think there are at least three reasons to be hopeful.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, for well over a decade, we have invested heavily in our CET infrastructure and embarked on the SkillsFuture movement since 2015.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We now have a very vibrant CET ecosystem that provides quality training to working adults, which we will continue to strengthen under the Next Bound of SkillsFuture.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When I meet with my international counterparts, this very well-developed CET eco-system and the SkillsFuture movement are a great source of envy for them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, even with low visibility, we are not navigating without compasses and searchlights.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For several years now, we have developed Industry Transformation Maps and carefully positioned each sector for future growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is the work of the Future Economy Council, which Deputy Prime Minister Heng chairs, and it has been investing a tremendous amount of time and effort to ensure that the roadmap to the future is well outlined at the very least and we know what we need to do.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: That makes for much more effective curation of training and attachment pathways.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A big push for these pathways will inspire hope and confidence in our people and keep us moving forward.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: She says poetically, "Life is not about waiting for the storm to pass.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It's about learning how to dance in the rain".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And along the way, if we also learn to dance in the rain, why not?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, on the Budgets being a responsive one and finetuning for maximum impact.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, our fiscal sustainability, reserves for next generation and shared responsibility in crisis.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And third, that this is a good time now to transform.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On the first point, responsive Budgets, finetuning for maximum impact.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We are now midway through the year 2020.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This pandemic has wreaked havoc in many ways around the world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Over 200 countries affected, more than six million infected and close to 400,000 deaths, so far.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Economists described this as equivalent to the Great Depression in the 1930s.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even some of my older residents told me that they had not experienced such hardship in decades.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I am grateful that our Government introduced four budgets to help our people cope with the hardship.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Each successive Budget responded to the latest development and the latest emerging need.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But it is clear that our Government wants to put cash into people's hands as soon as possible to reduce the pain.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Residents write to me to say how the rolling living and business expenses are "killing" them figuratively and mentally.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They know that the pandemic is a worldwide problem and appreciate the cash assistance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A self-employed home cleaner David told me that he could not work for three months and has to pay bills and rental.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, he has to give up the van at this moment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He is now desperately looking forward to resuming his work and start earning again.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: During the distribution of Government-issued masks, I met an 80-year-old uncle who is still raising his family.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He was crying as he told me about his job loss and his fears of being unable to see his son through school.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To see a man cry is hard, to see an elderly man cry is just heartbreaking.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many households that used to get by or used to do well are now under water.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When the help schemes were announced, many rejoiced.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But concerns also emerged as they tried to apply for it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Businesses appreciate the reprieve that this can offer.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But a resident Andy told me that when he and his peers realised they still have to pay significant interest during the deferment period, they all backed out.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In Andy's case, the deferment interest is more than the cash assistance he could get and there is no certainty whether his business will have a full recovery before the bank starts asking him to pay again.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This seems to defeat the purpose of having this facility, even for viable businesses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Such a situation will save companies with normally healthy cashflow, but perhaps not those that may have been or are planning to invest in strategic capabilities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There were still fears that the initial reliefs are not enough and some subtenants fear that waivers will not be passed down to them or that landlords will take a long time to do so.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But this will be addressed in the amendments to the Temporary Measures Act later, so this is great news!

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The reasons for contact tracing and using technology to do so are understandable.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But this is causing some difficulty for seniors to access certain essential services, because manual registration at present is only a guideline.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, my resident Yui Mun said that her mother and other elderly cannot enter the private clinics they usually go to, because they do not have smartphones with data plan to scan and register via SafeEntry.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The normal argument would have been to take the business elsewhere, but in this case, it is disruptive to switch as elderly usually have longstanding relationships with their GPs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Might there be ways to compel such operators to accommodate?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I urge the Government to continue finetuning the measures implemented, as we learn from experience and start stabilising.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The second point is really about fiscal sustainability, having reserves for next generation and sharing the responsibility in a crisis.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we battle this crisis, I am again thankful that our past and present leaders have been judicious in managing our reserves, painstakingly saving up for "storms" like this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Because of this, we can now confidently dip in to help Singaporeans – for the third time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This amount already exceeds the total full year public expenditure in 2019.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Looking around the world, only Japan and Singapore are able to pump in hefty stimulus packages.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Comparatively, others in our region may find it difficult to implement similar support packages.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some of our neighbours do not have deep reserves, and while they could reach loans with ultra-low interest rates, this could threaten their fiscal sustainability.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To give a sense of how much our Government is putting in to help Singaporeans and businesses, I did a back-of-envelope estimation of economic relief per capita – migrant not included – among developed countries.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are calculated based on publicly available figures.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These figures are coarse estimations taking into account direct and indirect support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But it gives us a very good sense of our Government's determination in supporting our people and seeing Singapore through this crisis.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Alas, this pandemic is expected to last for many more months and the world economy remains uncertain.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some experts think that the worst has yet to come.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I wonder how many more packages we will need and how much more might we have to dip into our reserves for.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Lest I get misunderstood, let me state that I believe it is necessary for us to draw on our reserves to help Singapore and Singaporeans get through this storm.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But I am concerned if we have enough to leave behind for our future generations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How can we sustain help and not deplete this pot of gold for our children and theirs?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our Pioneers took more than 50 years to save up this pot of gold because they want to protect their children and future generations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Similarly, we have a duty to use this pot of gold wisely and make sure that we put back what we took once we can, so that our children and their children will continue to have this asset to fall back on when they face the crisis of their generation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Will the Government assure us that it will do so?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To this end, I therefore think that it is important that we all shoulder the responsibility of overcoming this crisis together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government will draw from our treasury and reserves to provide the financial stimulus and put in place schemes and legislation to ensure fair distribution of help and boost sectors that are flailing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Businesses will have to do its best to survive and keep jobs for the workers; and workers need to be willing to accept concessions so that everyone can stay above water.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Landlords need to learn to share because they have a symbiotic relationship with tenants.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If the tenants fail, they may not find another and all will suffer.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the society level, the more abled need to be willing to take less and give more.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The less abled need to be willing to try their best to adjust, to change track, to upskill and to progress.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It would be quite difficult for the Government alone to eradicate all the pain for everyone, although it is trying.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If we can all be more accommodating, a bit more "give-and-take" and try a bit harder, we will have a good chance of succeeding together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: By sharing more is perhaps the only way to attain a more sustainable future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And onto my third point, that this is a good time now to transform.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On this note, as we look ahead, we can expect the world to change post COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is a tough time now, but since we are already in this predicament, there is also no better time to transform for the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: McKinsey, in a recent article, suggested that there will be seven key changes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, "distance is back" with technology enabling communications, work and trade being done without physical proximity.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, in strategising, businesses need to be able to absorb shock, on top of just being efficient.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, rise of the contact-free economy, including digital commerce, telemedicine and automation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Fourth, more Government intervention to ensure fairer distribution of precious resources.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Fifth, more scrutiny for businesses as they will increasingly be expected by the public to contribute more socially for the public good.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Sixth, industry structures, consumer behaviours, market positions and sector attractiveness will change.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And seventh, everyone is compelled to innovate to connect and solve problems in new ways.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In some instances, they may not find a way back to their old jobs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But there are new opportunities on the horizon.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But all these jobs will demand a new set of skills in the innovation and technology area.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, Singaporeans need to be prepared to train for it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Human capital and the quality of our talent pool will be a crucial differentiating factor for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In a recent encounter, a very wise elder and prominent business leader asked me about what I thought about the fourth industrial revolution.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I was a bit surprised as I am a junior but I suppose he just wanted to know how a younger person like me think about this issue.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, I shared that the digital future is inevitable and we all know why it is important.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I trust the Government to get the infrastructure, the big pieces right and ready.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But the quality of our people will decide whether Singapore continues to have a voice on the world stage.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If we do not have enough people with the right skills to fill these new jobs, investments can go away and we will all be for the poorer.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As countries around us step up, our talent pool must be ready earlier than them so that we can anchor these opportunities here in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Ultimately, it is the quality of our people that will determine if we can lead in this innovation race.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I am heartened that this fourth Budget not only addresses immediate needs, but also locked its vision on the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I hope this will be the final push to reach the tipping point for our SMEs to transform.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If this proves to be successful, I hope the bonus can be applied to other sectors in time to come as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I spoke about avoiding a new social divide inadvertently caused by our push for digitalisation in past years' debates.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On the ground, I have also been working with our grassroots to champion digital readiness for our seniors and low-income families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I hope we can press on and scale up.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: From observations, seniors who are digital converts are well placed to help other seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Similar in spirit to the digital resilience bonus, perhaps a digital wallet with e-cash vouchers would incentivise more seniors to give digital solutions a chance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And in the spirit of sharing responsibilities, local grassroots could explore strategic partnerships to raise funds and issue these vouchers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is doing the same thing but in a different way.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):  : COVID-19 is a major event that has changed the whole world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some experts are of the view that this pandemic has caused more harm than the Great Depression in the 1930s.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some residents in my constituency remarked that this was the most serious crisis they have seen in the past decades.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In this crisis, no one can be spared.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Everyone is facing a certain amount of challenges and sufferings.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many of my residents came to me for help.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is heart breaking to see that they are full of anxieties and are at a loss.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the pandemic evolves and demand changes, the Government has introduced 4 Budgets to help Singaporeans and businesses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must thank our forefathers for their hard work.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government has been flexible, and acted boldly and decisively to introduce a series of measures to revive the economy and assist the people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is much appreciated by the people and I agree with them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The fight against COVID-19 seems to be a prolonged battle.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I cannot help worrying whether our reserves, built up painstakingly over the years, will be depleted.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If our future generations were to face such situation, what are they going to rely upon?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In times of crisis, everyone could and should help to shoulder responsibilities, working in solidarity to overcome the difficulties.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government is setting aside a huge amount of money to revitalise the economy and help the people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Employers should do their best to keep the business going and retain their workers; Workers should cooperate with the company to make necessary adjustments.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Landlords should be compassionate to the tenants and give them some breathing space.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There will be many days ahead as long as we manage to survive this outbreak.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the community, the abled can make more sacrifices, and the beneficiaries should solider on with fortitude.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: By doing this, we will be able to achieve sustainability in the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I keep thinking of this poem "Grass" which says that "Grass in the wild are not thoroughly burned off; they will grow again in the spring".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I often recite this poem to my two sons.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I hope they can develop in them the same tenacious spirit as the wild grass.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He once said, "The tiny grass does not succumb to adversities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It does not feel inferior just because it is tiny.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is the spirit of a tiny grass." A sparkle can ignite a whole prairie; small streams can converge into rivers and oceans; a tiny seed can grow into a big tree, a small tiny screw can affect the performance of the entire machine.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We may feel that we are insignificant, but when united we can be very powerful.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Perhaps, this is what the Fortitude Budget seeks to achieve.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   Sir, COVID-19 has led to economic contraction all around the world and Singapore is no exception.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We have to thank the previous Governments for saving for a rainy day, progressively setting aside budget surpluses for our reserves.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The circuit breaker has just ended and every company hopes to resume operations as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Every employer is eager for his or her employees to resume work.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Every Singaporean hopes to resume their lifestyles like before, visiting their parents, shopping, and going to the park.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Currently, there is no cure nor vaccine for COVID-19, so we cannot do away with the preventive measures.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: So then how can we deal with the new normal in the post-circuit breaker period?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Will COVID-19 continue to spread in the community?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Perhaps, the testing of 39,000 pre-school staff can offer some clues.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Among the 14, 13 had contracted the virus previously and were no longer infectious at the point when they were confirmed as positive cases.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In other words, these 13 pre-school staff were not aware that they had been infected prior to testing.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Before they recovered, they could have passed the virus to others and spread it to the community while they were out and about.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Fortunately, they had gone out less during the circuit breaker period and have minimised the risk of infecting others.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: More importantly, among the 39,000 pre-school staff, one individual was infected recently.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: From the infection of pre-school staff, it is not difficult to understand why zero community infection could not be maintained in the past few weeks.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Moving forward, as we embark on the first phase of the post-circuit period, more people will leave home to work and the risk of community infection will definitely increase.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I know that many SMEs would like to resume operations but I would urge everyone to be more patient.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: On the other hand, our community infection rate has been relatively low.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There are only five patients in ICU currently.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Experts say that in the next one and a half years, it is not possible to eradicate COVID-19 totally from the community.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Therefore, Singaporeans must remain vigilant, wash their hands frequently, wear a mask and maintain the one metre safe distance.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Safe management measures at workplaces will become the new normal.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If people are infected, they should be quarantined immediately, and proactive contact tracing must be conducted.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If people are able to accept this new normal and understand that COVID-19 will not disappear in a few months like SARS, I hope MTF will allow all industries to resume operations as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Otherwise, no matter how much support and grants are given, so long as companies cannot operate, there will still be retrenchments and insolvencies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I believe that the Government will be flexible in this aspect.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I am the advisor of the Renovation Contractors’ Associations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The Chairman of the Association, its key members and myself have held meetings with BCA several times to pave the way for resuming work.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many families’ renovation projects had to stop because of the circuit breaker measures, and they cannot wait for the project to start again.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, the requirements for resumption of renovation projects have been very stringent.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Through several rounds of consultations, BCA has simplified the procedures and allowed several thousand renovation projects to resume on 2 June.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: COVID-19 has disrupted industries and sped up the pace of digital transformation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, at markets and hawker centres, most stallholders accept cash only.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: After NETs was set up in 1985, Singapore soon became the leader for e-payments in Asia.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There are also plans to recruit 1,000 digital ambassadors to help the elderly Singaporeans learn digital skills.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Last year, when organising the River Hongbao activities, we worked with NETS to encourage the food stallholders to adopt cashless payments.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: When I visited markets, hawker centres and coffeeshops, I also received feedback on cashless payments from stallholders.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Therefore, I would like to make a few suggestions so that we can improve the e-payment adoption rate and the efficiency of digital ambassadors.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Some stallholders are worried about the cash flow problem, so they hope that they will be able to get the e-payments by customers several hours after the payments were made.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Stallholders currently pay cash to suppliers for materials.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If this segment of the supply chain can be digitised, more stallholders may be encouraged to adopt e-payment.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There are currently 19 e-payment platforms in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I understand that the intention of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) is to allow different e-payment platforms to thrive.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This will make e-payment easier for Singaporeans, especially the elderly.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: According to a report by Lianhe Zaobao, most of the digital ambassadors recruited will be graduates from Institutes of Higher Learning (IHL).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: These fresh graduates are familiar with technology, but they may not empathise with the fear and resistance of stallholders against e-payments.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I hope that the Government will focus more on recruiting Singaporeans who may have initial reservations about technology but have learnt to use e-payment eventually.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Then, they can effectively encourage stallholders to embark on digital transformation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The Chinese say that food is the most important of all things.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Only when everyone can use e-payment to buy food, can we say that our digital transformation is truly taking shape.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I hope that from now onwards, stallholders who used to count cash will use the QR code as the norm.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, resilience is forged through crisis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: While COVID-19 has created havoc, it is clear that COVID-19 has also brought out the best in us, not just in putting the community above self-interest and abiding by the circuit breaker rules, but also in how some of us are extending a helping hand to others.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There are countless examples, like those who have volunteered to help out in the frontline at the migrant worker dormitories, or those who have signed up with different charities via Giving.sg to donate money, essential items or volunteer their time.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There are also many inspiring stories in Jurong West, helping others during this difficult time.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: One of our residents, Joyce Yu, did not throw up her hands in defeat when her parent's nasi lemak hawker stall suffered from a plunge in business due to COVID-19 and the circuit breaker measures.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Instead, she managed to raise funds from her friends so that her parents could provide nasi lemak as free breakfast for needy families in Jurong.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As her parents also had hawker friends who were in the same situation, she slowly expanded the scheme.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Grassroots volunteers also chipped in by distributing the food free of charge.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Joyce has a full-time job with YMCA but she is happy to liaise with the hawkers and raise funds.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: She says she wanted to come up with a scheme which is a win-win solution to support local businesses, hawkers like her mother's, while feeding vulnerable people.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We want to collect all these good deeds and inspire more to follow.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This year National Day will not have the glitter and pageantry of the huge parades like what we have had over the last 54 years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This year's National Day is our nation's 55th birthday.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We want to celebrate the unsung heroes fighting the COVID-19, the everyday resilience and the sense of community on the ground which has given us a silver lining during these challenging times.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But, we are also want to be the pioneers that transform our economy digitally so that our children can reap the fruits of our new digital economy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In the fight against COVID-19, I hope all Singaporeans can proudly say “count on me”.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This programme is especially timely as our country goes through rapid digitalisation, now fiercely accelerated by COVID-19.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As mature workers, mid-career jobseekers are understandably anxious about the drastic confluence of digital disruptions, outmoded skills and ageism working against them.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Compared to fresh graduates, their needs are more complex as many would also be from the sandwich class, juggling lifestage obligations of parenting and eldercare and so their salary expectations are naturally higher.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Even though they have an established track record, they will find it harder to pivot, having honed their skills in industries that may be on the decline.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: And yet, with their maturity and life experience, they still have much to offer our society and ample potential to grow.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As the relevant Ministries and agencies work together to operationalise the finer details of this programme, I would like to share insights from industry leaders so that the programme can bring maximum benefit to the trainees and companies participating in this scheme.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The participating companies’ should be supported with instructive guidelines on how best to integrate and upskill their trainees.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: For example, career portal Mums@Work has successfully experimented with developing consortia of companies in related industries collaborating to collectively train returning talents so that they can be exposed to a broader swathe of skills.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Trainees can thus explore multiple career paths and better identify their transferable strengths in the process.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: With such innovative arrangements, companies can offer their trainees a wider range of skills upgrading opportunities and support each other without incurring prohibitive overheads.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: They should also be more explicit about articulating their criteria for retention if they can afford to increase their headcount.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: That way, the trainees will not feel like they have been led down the garden path.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Besides such substantive issues, the approach that participating companies adopt in hosting these trainees can also make or break a traineeship.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: There are horror stories of job attachment schemes where mature trainees must sign in daily for a visitor’s pass to enter the company, or who are supervised by very junior colleagues with no managerial experience to speak of.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: These socio-emotional aspects of mid-career training must be effectively addressed to ensure win-win outcomes for everyone.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Above all, the scheme must accord trainees with a sense of purpose and dignity.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: On their part, trainees must also pull their weight and not regard the traineeship as a paid sabbatical.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: They too should be provided with pointers on how they can make the most of their stints and the appropriate mind sets they should adopt to fully benefit from the programme.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Fundamentally, the traineeships should offer a combination of substantive skills and career planning competencies that will empower these mid-career jobseekers for their next career move.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, the experience of the Singapore Computer Society’s Career Compass programme offers some valuable lessons.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: With a careful and concerted design of SGUnited Mid-Career Traineeship offerings and actionable guidelines for participating companies and trainees, I am hopeful that this scheme can help to prepare mid-career workers for the next phase of their careers.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: On that optimistic note, I support the Fortitude Budget.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is an unprecedented Budget but it is necessary as this is one of the worst crises to hit us in our nation’s history.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of my residents in Henderson-Dawson have shared with me how they and their companies have been directly assisted by the various assistance schemes and programmes announced as parts of the Unity, Resilience and Solidarity Budgets.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many are also acutely aware that we are drawing on our reserves and have expressed their worries about drawing down on our nation’s savings, especially since we do not know how long this crisis will last.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is a delicate balance between the needs of our present and our future, and the Government has had to make some very tough decisions for the good of everyone in Singapore under these trying circumstances.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am glad to see that the various age groups of our society will continue to receive assistance.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: From young graduates to middle aged employees, and to older workers, all will receive help with jobseeking, job-matching and training.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We are especially concerned for the sandwiched workers – those who are supporting both children and elderly parents.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I urge them to take up the various assistance schemes applicable to them and come forward to request for help if they are unsure of what to do.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is important that even as we focus on taking care of our immediate needs, we must also be mindful of our external environment and keep an eye on what is ahead of us.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In early May, Deputy Prime Minister Heng had said that, I quote, “there should be no lost generation in Singapore… we are sailing into uncharted waters, surveying the new landscape, exploring new growth and opportunities, preparing to seize them when the storm passes..." I would like to speak a little about the young adults who will be joining or who had just joined our workforce.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a world that seems so familiar and yet so different from the one they had grown up expecting to enter.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This generation had grown up hearing from their elders about how fortunate they have been, growing up enjoying the many benefits of a prosperous nation as compared to Singapore’s founding years.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And now suddenly, within the space of a few months, the world has changed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is so much harder for them to get jobs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Suddenly, we also have an entire generation of Romeos and Juliets, forbidden from meeting each other.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, for some young people, the jobs they had been preparing for may have all but disappeared and some are even at a loss about whether they should consider switching industries.Thus, the Government, together with industry and the Institutes of Higher Learning, should work even more closely together to help them navigate the job market in this challenging environment.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must be mindful of the impact of this crisis on them for years to come and have the appropriate strategy to help them to ensure that they will not become a lost or traumatised generation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For a number of them, they are entering the adult world with “empty hands”, as their parents and family members may also face job losses or business difficulties.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My concern is that as our economy recovers in the future, this cohort’s experience and their subsequent actions would have consequences for us as a nation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even with the use of technology and solemnisations via video link, relationships and marriages may be delayed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They may delay having children, have fewer children or none at all.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In delaying procreation, the chances of having healthy children are reduced.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our family units form the foundation of our society.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Matching up young single Singaporeans may hardly be a priority now but I hope the Government will be mindful of this issue as it has wide ranging implications, including our economy’s competitiveness and national security.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As for those who have decided to take the leap, we can do more to support these new young families.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are attractive grants in place for HDB flat purchases.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Please consider accepting even lower deposits and smaller repayments monthly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The crisis will not last forever, in three to five years, the economy will pick up and the couples can make up for the difference later.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will also be timely as they progress in their careers, earn more and become able to afford higher mortgage payments.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also wish to appeal for higher subsidies for pregnancy check-ups, deliveries and childhood vaccinations to make procreation even more affordable.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would MND also consider building bigger HDB flats in the future?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Not only do bigger units allow families to continue living together and help to look after each other, they will also take into account that more citizens will be working and studying online from home.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us support our young adults who are standing at the entrance of independence and parenthood.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Encourage them to proceed to the next lap with those they love.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And throughout the way, we will help everyone to tide through these tough times together.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has brought with it a health and economic crisis that has Singapore facing the worst recession since Independence.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is indeed a blessing that Singapore should possess such a reservoir of financial resources to see us through this crisis.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many countries around the world will be burdened, burdened in the years to come with record levels of debt from the huge fiscal stimulus programmes they have had to put in place to deal with the impact from COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But, Sir, there is no question that Singapore was absolutely right to tap the reserves decisively in order to help businesses, tide Singaporeans through this crisis and mitigate permanent damage to our economy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, we should also be concerned about fiscal sustainability, especially when the outlook remains uncertain and downside risks remain significant.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There is a lot of talk about what would the shape of the recovery be, but many believe that recovery will be slow and long-drawn; it may take years before we return to pre-COVID-19 conditions.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Against this backdrop, I wonder how this massive draw on our reserves will be treated.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To do so, would be a huge task as the amount is more than 10 times our previous draw, when we used it to deal with the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How will this influence our tax policy in the coming years, as we work to restore public finances in an equitable manner?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Will we need to dig deeper, to implement more progressive income taxes and greater wealth taxes?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Will tax systems need to evolve in tandem with the rising digital economy and capture revenue earned from online transactions?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I urge Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat to adopt in the next phase, if he has to do something, a more targeted approach in future support schemes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For example, the Jobs Support Scheme (JSS), payouts should only go to firms adversely impacted by the crisis.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In Australia, for their scheme, eligibility for wage support only kicks in if business turnover drops by 30% due to the pandemic; for larger companies with turnovers of over A$1 billion, their drop in turnover must be at least 50% before they can be eligible.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It should not be right for firms to profit from the Government's support scheme during this crisis.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For some companies, whose bottom lines have been boosted because of JSS, they should be offered the opportunity to "pay it forward", in support of others who are less fortunate, perhaps through a "Solidarity Levy" of some sort.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Recent research at Oxford found that those earning under GBP20,000 are less able to perform work remotely, earn a smaller proportion of their previous salary and are twice as likely to lose their jobs compared to those earning GBP40,000 or more.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We can draw similar parallels here in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It has been far easier for those employed by large companies and highly skilled sectors to work remotely, than for those employed by SMEs or in the retail and F&B sectors, as well as those engaged in low-paying contract work.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, we must find ways to buffer the hardship faced by these families.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We should be prepared to support them with some basic level of income beyond the current provision of COVID-19 Support Grant, should their unemployment persist.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister has promised to "protect every worker even if we cannot protect every job".

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But this commitment to protect every worker should not create a false sense of security or complacency.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Instead, it should encourage individuals to leverage this safety net in order to position themselves for the longer term, by critically assessing their operating environment, learn new skills, try new jobs and seize on the many schemes available to ensure that they remain relevant.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The formation of National Jobs Council as well as the Emerging Stronger Task Force are great initiatives for developing strategies to pivot ourselves to the new jobs landscape.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I am also impressed with the speed by which job initiatives are being rolled out – these include the 11,000 traineeships by 1,000 organisations who have come on board so far, so quite impressive.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Our ability to coordinate, navigate and implement Whole-of-Government initiatives is truly the competitive advantage that Singapore must play to.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is a testament of the confidence that investors and businesses have in Singapore and the hard work that MTI continues to put into selling "Singapore Inc".

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, our response to the pandemic shone a light on the meaningful work that healthcare professionals do and held them up as the heroes that they have always been.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: School children wrote "thank you" notes, Prime Ministers called them out and people clapped from their balconies the world over, out of gratitude for their sacrifice.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I must say I am so encouraged to witnessed an emerging interest amongst young people in joining the healthcare industry and shifting attitudes towards the care-giving profession.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Lastly, COVID-19 has taught us that large-scale remote working is indeed possible.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With the help of technology, employers are quickly equipping their workers with the tools they need to work from home.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I myself have been surprised at how much more productive I have been, working away from the office.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Facebook has begun planning for workers to work permanently from home, whilst Google has extended its work-from-home policy for the remainder of 2020.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many tech firms complain that they have not been able to scale their business in Singapore given our limited talent pool.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, extend that, work from home, but beyond the national borders.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore companies can tap AI, data analytics, cybersecurity resources from around the world to support Singapore's development work without these tech professionals having to relocate to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Winston Churchill is credited with first saying, "Never let a good crisis go to waste".

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore has certainly invested a good deal in this crisis, it is time to learn the lessons, turn challenges into opportunities and reap the rewards for a stronger, brighter tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am also thankful for all the hard work by MOM, all the other Government agencies and the NGOs who have worked tirelessly to help our migrant friends.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I raised all these concerns in my previous speeches and I am thankful to everyone who has taken the time to share your concerns, feedback and suggestions with me.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can and we need to give time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Time for working parents to spend with and look after their young children during this difficult period.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: During this pandemic, many parents are feeling the stress of trying to balance work and looking after their children, especially helping their young ones with home-based learning (HBL).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Zack, a parent, shared with me, "Imagine working from 9.00 am to 6.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And only having this time, 7.30 pm to 9.00 pm, to check on the kids' HBL.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Kids must sleep at 9.00 pm to ensure nine hours of healthy sleep.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, we endured for the sake of our children".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many parents are especially worried about how they will cope with alternating weeks of HBL for non-graduating students.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It will be difficult for parents who are unable to work from home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Not everyone has grandparents who can help and even for those who do, they might not be able to help during this period.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another parent shared with me, "I have two Primary school going kids.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Who is available to guide them on HBL days during Phase One?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If there isn’t any HBL plus Google meet plus video call, I will choose to deposit them at my parents house easily.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If I have to take annual leave to guide their HBL, employer won’t allow." I know Minister Ong has stated, "Schools will be prepared to extend limited care to young students on HBL but without childcare arrangements".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It will also be difficult for parents who can work from home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are expected to meet their bosses' deadline and to be equally productive, even as they try to give their young ones attention and guide them on HBL.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Do they please their employers or the children?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For the past two months, I worked from home with three little ones who had HBL.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ella is now six years old and Katie and Poppy are three years old.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: You cannot leave them to do HBL on their own.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They have also attended many of my Zoom work meetings, climbed on my shoulders when I am clearing emails, and pulled my hands and legs, wanting me to play with them when I am drafting speeches.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This happened when I was drafting this speech last Saturday.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Parents truly appreciate this opportunity to work from home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Zyen, another parent, shared, “WFH with an infant is really no joke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Always have to work till midnight to complete the work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I‘ve been there when she flipped, sat up by herself and now standing with support.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am not the only one with kids climbing on my shoulders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Amelia shared that, “My son climbs onto my shoulders while I work, too.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I feel guilty for being impatient with my daughter who asks questions or wants to share something with me while I’m rushing my work”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know there is no easy solution, especially during these difficult times.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we need to give parents some breathing space and help them balance both work and family commitments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is good that the Government has asked employers to be more empathetic to the challenges working parents face but we need to do more than that.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We cannot leave this important issue to the discretion of the employer.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government needs to step in to help and to mandate like how we have done so in so many areas in tackling this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to remember the issue does not just stem from alternating weeks of HBL.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What about parents whose children are required to stay home because they are exhibiting COVID-like symptoms?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many pre-schools rightly ask a child to go home if he or she shows a single symptom.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But a lot of parents are affected because of this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: An educator in a childcare centre shared with me that, “On the ground, parents tend to negotiate with teachers if teachers were to reject children from entering schools due to respiratory symptoms with reasons that they are unable to get leave from work or no one to take care of their children”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some parents, “would suggest to teachers to keep children at the sick bay the entire day until the parents end work”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us not forget that there are also school closures due to positive COVID-19 cases, Leave of Absence or Stay-Home Notices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Now, in the most irregular year, how can parents possibly have sufficient childcare leave?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, many parents have shared that they are doing just that.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But in this business climate, parents fear losing their jobs if they continue to take unpaid leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To help parents, I hope we can introduce a Government-paid COVID-19-related childcare leave for parents whose children need to stay home due to COVID-19-related issues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By calling for it to be Government-paid, this would ease the financial burden for employers, whom I know are equally stressed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This includes parents working in essential services who perform a duty for our nation, who keep us safe.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to make sure that they are looked after, too.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For parents who are working from home, this COVID-19-related childcare leave can help take off the pressures of balancing competing work and childcare responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They can take this leave when needed, such as helping their child catch up with HBL and their school work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Other countries have already taken steps to help working parents facing childcare challenges as a result of this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Businesses whose employees take this leave pay for it through a refundable tax credit administered by the Department of Treasury.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means working half time or one day off a week, taken in any combination of weekly or monthly blocks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Other countries have adopted a variety of measures – tax credits, protection against discriminatory firing, increase in annual leave and flexible leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe some combination of these solutions would provide our working parents the support they so desperately need.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this difficult time, the Government has to step in.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many parents are calling for this and I hope the Government will support them. “Spend time with those you love, one of these days you will either say I wish I had or I’m glad I did.” Let us give our working parents the time they need to spend with their children during this pandemic and let us all value the precious time we have with our loved ones.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I also appreciate the sensitive consideration of naming each Budget such that we are emotionally connected to them. "Fortitude" is an excellent name for this Budget as we dig deep into courage to face the painful effects of an unfolding economic crisis.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Many have reached out to me with their stories.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Witnessing this suffering has compelled me to file cuts tomorrow, so that the issues faced by struggling groups are raised to this House.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The number of households who have suffered complete loss of income since the beginning of April has risen sharply.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: On the ground, community organisations have observed that households face mounting debt, including rent arrears.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As the economic impact of COVID-19 worsens, we can expect that more households residing in rental flats will struggle to pay rent.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This will provide immediate and targeted relief that goes directly to the low-income households in need.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A further $2 billion will offset SMEs’ rental costs..

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The World Economic Forum has called turbulence “the new normal” in its latest Global Risks Report.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I will focus on the long term in this speech.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The hard work of Singaporeans and Singapore companies, as well as prudent financial management of our Reserves, has allowed us to save up for this rainy day.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is only fiscally responsible for us to ensure that we spend the monies to build a stronger foundation for this new turbulent normal.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This demands that we push boundaries and reimagine a social and economic structure that is more responsive, flexible and interconnected.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I will then discuss the considerations in our current spending and planning processes that can set us on the path towards this stronger, more sustainable and more inclusive future.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng mentioned that this Budget’s focus is to “enable our businesses and workers to adapt, transform and seize new opportunities”.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, but even more so, our society and economy need a deep transformation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The COVID-19 crisis has shown us unequivocally that human health is intrinsically linked to planetary health.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Our increasing urbanisation and disruption of ecological balances increase our risks of exposure to pathogens.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, the Clinicians for Planetary Health initiative was launched.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It committed to increase awareness of the severe public health impacts of environmental change.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, it is safe to say that to safeguard our economic future, the balance of resources across people, planet and profit needs to be re-examined.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, we can no longer look at our risk response in silo.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Risks are multi-dimensional and cross-cutting, and must be addressed as such.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Our healthcare system had integrated and implemented the playbook from SARS well – only 3.1% of our infections had been healthcare workers so far, compared to 41% for SARS.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, systemic gaps in worker welfare, specifically for migrant workers, left us unprepared for the infection levels in the dormitories.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The risk assessment framework should have included the adequacy of safeguards for worker health.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This would have required MOH and MOM to work together.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Second, existing societal inequities create disproportionate stresses on vulnerable communities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: My previous speeches provided several examples of persons with mental health conditions, lower income households and migrant workers being disproportionately affected in terms of income loss and economic and psychological resilience.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The digital divide amongst lower income families, the differently-abled and the elderly became more evident.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: All these could deepen social and community fault lines.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: What does all this mean in terms of transformation?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I call for Singapore to move towards multi-stakeholderism.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Governance-wise, this means a policy design process centred around and in collaboration with the actors with a “stake” in the outcome.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Business-wise, it means considering workers, suppliers and customers equally.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The World Economic Forum was established in 1971 to further the idea that business should serve all stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A hundred and eighty one CEOs of the Business Roundtable signed a statement last year, committing “to lead their companies for the benefit of all stakeholders – customers, employees, suppliers, communities and shareholders.” Investors also value businesses that take care of its stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In April 2020, the International Corporate Governance Network (ICGN) led by investors responsible for assets of $54 trillion called for companies to “prioritise employee safety and welfare” and “take a holistic and equitable approach to capital allocation decisions, considering the workforce”.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng alluded to similar sentiments in parts of his speech.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Government’s strategy to help Singaporeans ride through this crisis is by safeguarding jobs and income, which it is doing by supporting businesses.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has also provided support through enabling credit access and matching investments for start-ups.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Reducing inequality would also increase resilience across our society, especially in times of hardship, so that economic buffers and important resources do not become accessible only to the privileged few.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, we must enact measures to protect individuals against employers who may be more interested in self-enrichment than in their workers’ rice bowls.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Possible measures are curbs on layoffs, excessive executive compensation, and excessive use of share options in compensation structures that disproportionately align managers only to shareholders’ interests.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Government bailouts and support may reduce shareholders’ risk-bearing responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Measuring and reporting should be used to hold companies accountable for how they have used Government grants, therefore taxpayers’ monies.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: An example is the independent accountability and transparency board created by the Obama administration in 2009.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It performed a crucial monitoring function by requiring any entity receiving contracts, grants, or loans to file quarterly reports.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We could adopt a similar mechanism to ensure that companies channel Government support to those for whom it is intended.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Corporate reporting requirements could compel companies to demonstrate behaviours that meet broader societal and sustainability goals.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must also use the support packages as carrots for companies to actively enhance social equity by integrating community engagement and social responsibility into business strategy, so each can be a Company of Good – a national effort I believe Deputy Prime Minister is very familiar with.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This could include an obligation to judiciously use the Business and IPC Partnership Scheme or BIPs, to make in-kind donations to charities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, promoting sustainable business models will be key to building a better and safer future.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: McKinsey noted in April that “not only does climate action remain critical over the next decade, but investments in climate-resilient infrastructure and the transition to a lower carbon future can drive significant near-term job creation while increasing economic and environmental resiliency.” The President of the German Parliament recently called for the stimulus plan to focus on “climate policy, digitisation and innovation”.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As countries grapple with what a green and healthy recovery looks like, measurement and accountability may again be instrumental for change.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Task Force of Climate-related Financial Disclosures framework should be the norm.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Science-based targets should form the basis of discussions on business transformations.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Such requirements could be considered by the Monetary Authority of Singapore as a cornerstone of future environment risk management guidelines for our financial industry.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These safeguards will require strong political will, Mr Deputy Speaker, because they will meet with resistance.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: But if we want a flexible and responsive society that is able to absorb shocks and rebound from them, I believe we must recalibrate current power structures for a fairer economy that considers key stakeholders in our economic system equally.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I hope Deputy Prime Minister addresses this need for safeguards and conditions in his response.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Government is demonstrating its commitment to longer term planning through the Emerging Stronger Task Force and the Future Economy Council.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, if we are to recognise a wide range of stakeholders in our future and commit to re-imagining the way forward, changes must be made.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad to hear Deputy Prime Minister note that the Task Force will partner with SME owners, industry experts and trade associations as part of Emerging Stronger and his invitation for Singaporeans to participate.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is necessary to integrate meaningful and transparent input from all corners of society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The current members of the Task Force represent industries that we have traditionally treated as pillars of our current economic structure, the composition does not represent the true diversity of economic players in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For example, I am surprised by the omission of SME, minority, even disability and mental health representation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Companies committed to delivering a sustainable future are also unrepresented, under-represented.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
