text: I believe that if we sideline these views now, we are sabotaging our own futures and those of our children’s.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The names of the four extraordinary Budgets this year speak to our desire as a nation to overcome this crisis together and stronger.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All governments around the world are taking unprecedented measures to mitigate the damaging impact of this outbreak and save the lives and livelihoods of their people.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fortunately, we have managed to keep most of our people here safe and the death rate low.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a challenging war against the virus.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is different from other outbreaks that we have come across so far.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To my understanding, it is infectious even a person has not developed any symptoms.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Asymptomatic infections have made this task of overcoming it even more challenging and difficult.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding, we have to soldier on under these very trying circumstances, be resilient, stay united and help one another to overcome the obstacles ahead of us.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We Singaporeans need to stay focused on a sustainable approach.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By and large, we understand there is a limit to the handouts we can if we do not find sustainable income that provide long term and permanent social and family safety nets.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   I am heartened by the effort to save and create jobs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that more jobs can be created for the middle and senior age groups, particularly quality jobs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened by the response of our residents to the job offers, their willingness and courage in picking up new skills and adapting.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad that the Government has been focused on helping Singaporeans to both upskill and become equipped with new skills, to stay competitive and relevant in response to the market changes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is a Chinese saying “When rowing a boat upstream, if one does not move forward, the boat will go backwards downstream”.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our people must persist in their efforts forward so that we can secure our place in the world.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More assistance will still need to be given to help Singaporeans, as the recovery of the world economy may not be so fast.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For those who were retrenched last year and earlier, and had not been able to find jobs, they need help with job matching and retraining.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is especially for those aged above 40.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, some have expressed concerns that even with training, it does not necessarily lead to a job.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singaporeans should also adapt to tap upon technology and target not just Singapore, but the world as their market.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Recently, a Singaporean actor took on a side job selling seafood for his friends on the Internet.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To everyone’s surprise, including himself, he became an Internet celebrity, and companies and talent agencies from China rushed to contact him as their partner, asking him to promote all kinds of goods on the Internet.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a very popular way of selling goods in China’s huge market today.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While some of his language may be too colourful, his adaptability had created new opportunities for him.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: He can look forward to a very interesting new career.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Singapore, the Government has already started helping stallholders sell online and do live-streaming sales.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us hope more business owners will try to change their operating models.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There has been feedback that there are still many who have been struggling with their businesses and who have been making sacrifices for the circuit breaker to the extent that they have been lending to their companies with their pay to support cashflow.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some are concerned that their businesses may not pick up after the reopening of our economy and thus will continue to face financial difficulty.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important to them that all their clients order can be resumed.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Otherwise, such business cannot hang on much longer.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even with the salary support from the Government, many businesses cannot afford to pay the balance 25% because they have zero revenue.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we need to prioritise safety, and indeed, being a highly interconnected hub, we can only be safe if the world is also safe, however, we cannot be closed off from the world.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It will do more harm than good to “de-globalise”.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have to be proactive, not passive, to overcome this challenge.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In order to survive, we cannot afford to sit back and keep drawing upon our past reserves and assets.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, we could consider staycations now that our community infection rate has been controlled.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should also start thinking how we could have effective and efficient test kits to check on all inbound travellers and returnees to prevent imported cases while revitalising the aviation, tourism and MICE sectors.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Most importantly, those who have the ability should help the have-nots.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because everyone is important and we care for all.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: January: Complain about having to start work again February: Panic buying of paper products March: Causeway closed April: Everyone stayed home May: Resumption of work we hope June: Worry about savings being depleted July: Pray all will go smoothly August: Celebrate victory With this, I would like to conclude with my support for this Budget.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Twenty-twenty is a year to reset, regroup and relearn.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is both a health crisis and an economic crisis that affects our life, our health and how we live our lives.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But far beyond our personal spheres, the world is rapidly changing.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Tensions near and far, threaten to destabilise our once predictable place in the world.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Global supply chains are also changing as countries ramp up their "nationalistic" strategies.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Singapore has always depended on free and open trade.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We need to regroup and strategise what is next for us, what can steer our economy into the future where businesses can thrive and individuals can progress.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Other countries are also gradually ramping up their economies as they emerge out of lockdowns.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We need to swiftly identify the economic shifts and strategise the way forward.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister for Finance shed some light on the work done so far and its first findings?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: How can we take advantage of new opportunities and accelerate our economic rebound?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We are also likely to be able to retire later as technology allows us to work from home.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This COVID-19 pandemic has also affected seniors in many ways.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: These impacts have also been felt by our seniors, many of whom now communicate with video calls using WhatsApp or Zoom – something unheard of in 2019.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some seniors are also learning to shop online.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As we forge ahead in our new post-COVID-19 world, I anticipate far more online participation by our seniors than ever before.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: How can we capitalise on this digital transformation?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: How can we enable our seniors to be less isolated, more engaged with each other and with our society?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What can we do with technology to help seniors connect with their families and friends and continue contributing to society and the economy even as they continue to earn a wage?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is great that the Government is reaching out to help bridge our digital divide and at the same time provide employment opportunities for our graduating cohorts of ITE, Polytechnics and Universities.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I hope MCI will continue to accelerate our digitisation efforts post-COVID-19.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There is no doubt what we are experiencing is unprecedented.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I hope when we look back to this period in the future, we can say we overcame COVID-19 with unity, solidarity, resilience and fortitude.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He and hon Members who spoke before me, highlighted the deteriorating economic situation globally as well as in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Against this deteriorating situation, I am heartened that Deputy Prime Minister Heng made good his promise made in this House when he was delivering the Ministerial Statement on the Resilience Budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said, "should it become necessary, I am prepared to propose to the President further draws on past reserves to deal with the situation." Our past reserves has been characterised as our trump card to get out of this crisis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Indeed, it is fortunate that we can draw on our past reserves, thanks to the prudence of previous generations of Government Leaders and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But equally, it is fortunate that Singapore can count on two further trump cards.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They are: our exceptional people, who are all united in the common goal of defeating this virus and its effects on our health and economy; and our excellent men and women of the civil service.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: By civil service, I also include our Statutory Boards and our uniformed Services.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to record my appreciation to the officers in these Government agencies who have been working tirelessly throughout this crisis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We all know our civil service is a lean organisation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With the formulation and implementation of numerous Government budgetary programmes and measures as well as legislation passed in this House within short periods of time, these officers had to rapidly adapt and assume even more responsibilities to support Singaporeans during this turbulent period.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I, like a good number of hon Members have received reply emails from Government agencies on petitions written on behalf of residents promptly, despite a spike in the numbers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Many of these replies are received well after office hours.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Government agencies and partners dealing with applications to draw on the Government's COVID-19 support programmes do not have an easy task at all.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They need to strike a balance between providing help to fellow Singaporeans, ensuring that the policy objectives of the programmes and legislation are achieved and satisfying themselves that the public resources are judiciously spent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, I am delighted to note that more and more, our Government agencies apply a degree of flexibility in assessing applications.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our civil service is also transforming in its delivery efforts to better serve fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When we and our nation recover from this crisis, we should not forget the services of our men and women in civil service who went beyond their call of duty.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my view, it is not enough to pat them on their backs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We must follow up and provide tangible compensation to them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I made a similar call for our heroic frontline officers in my speech during the debate on the Unity Budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, providing a permanent legal framework to help small businesses in crises, like the one we currently face.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, encouraging the stakeholders in the charity sector to collaborate more so as to deliver more impactful programmes for Singaporeans who need help.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And finally, providing more credit and cash flow assistance to middle income families.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This measure deals with a big bugbear on the ground, given that most businesses in commercial premises have been closed for two months and are likely to be closed for at least a few more weeks.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng mentioned that this was not an easy decision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said "Government does not ordinarily intervene in contracts after they have been entered into".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I appreciate the point Deputy Prime Minister Heng made.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was the stance that was taken on behalf of the Government when I spoke on my Adjournment Motion "Power Imbalance in Contracts Involving Small Businesses" on the 5 February 2018.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Then, I argued for Government intervention in form of legislation to protect small businesses to equalise their bargaining positions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I highlighted clauses in tenancy agreements that operate unfairly against tenants which are small businesses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also drew examples of legislation being enacted in a number of advanced jurisdictions to help small businesses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Senior Minister of State for Law as she then was, Ms Indranee Rajah stated as follows: "In Singapore, our underlying philosophy is that, in general, free-market principles should apply and the Government should intervene only when necessary, for example, to address systemic market failure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Even when we do so, we try as far as possible to have the right regulatory touch and avoid heavy-handed interventions that could lead to distortion or unintended consequences".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To illustrate the point, let us consider the important role the Price Control Act, an act which the Deputy Speaker is very familiar with, played during the crisis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Price Control Act or PCA was enacted in 1950 to control prices of goods and to prevent price gouging.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was engaged in 1973 to fix the price of rice when it rose as a result panic buying, in the wake of the oil crisis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is also used in 1990 when the pork market was reportedly cornered by a few suppliers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, this is a lever that can be used when sellers take advantage of the situation created by crises.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Between January and February 2020, hon Members will recall that there was a public outcry against unscrupulous sellers taking advantage of the COVID-19 outbreak to sell surgical masks, thermometers and hand sanitisers at grossly inflated prices.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Price Controller took swift action under powers vested in him under PCA by requiring the sellers to provide information on the basis for setting prices at that level and also visiting the premises.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The issues were quickly resolved without the need for the Price Controller to exercise his power to fix the price of masks, thermometers and hand sanitizers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Across the Causeway, the government used powers under the equivalent of the PCA to fix the price of surgical masks.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is because the Government of the day can leverage on legislation to ensure that these small businesses will not go belly up in the face of similar crises in future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Significant business disruption to such small businesses can be irreversible.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There will also be the salutary signalling effect within the business community, as we saw in the case of masks sellers who self-regulated after the Price Controller launched queries into their business conduct.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do appreciate that the shape, form and impact of crises in future may be different.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The help measures may also differ from crisis to crisis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, this need not mean that a permanent piece of legislation would lose relevance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However different the crises may be, the impact on small businesses in form of cashflow and cost will largely remain.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For clarity's sake, the circumstances when Government's powers to intervene in the rental market may be triggered must also be spelt out too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The legislation may be worded broadly to provide for a wide spectrum of measures that the Government may impose to help our small businesses as we saw in the PCA example.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I respectfully suggest that the Emerging Stronger Task Force of the Future Economy Council consider my proposal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My next point concerns the support under the Fortitude Budget provided to the charity sector.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my speech during the debate on the Resilience and Solidarity Budgets, I highlighted the fact that some charities, especially the smaller ones, already were facing dwindling donations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I recall the hon Member, Mr Saktiandi also made the same point.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, we differed in the approach to be taken to deal with this problem.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member, Mr Saktiandi suggested that the Government support the charities; I felt chary about this suggestion because of the Budget deficit we face this year and the fact that we are drawing on past reserves.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It incentivises donations and the same time provides much needed support to charitable organisations in the essential service or providing the vulnerable a helping hand.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under this approach, there would be need for an analysis on the impact of the charitable programmes on the beneficiaries such that the more impactful programmes should be provided with more public funding.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There should be also financial incentives for charities to collaborate, pool resources and scale up.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng had noted that many individuals and organisations have stepped up to his call to help Singaporeans in need.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With the increased number of charitable funds and individuals wanting to do charity work, there is an opportunity get charitable organisations with similar ideals and objectives to work together to ensure that the dollar provided by our Government is better spent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It may well be that our Government will have to deepen its capability to play the role of matchmaker in encouraging charitable organisations to work together.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will, in my view, accelerate the transformation of the charity sector so that it will emerge stronger from this crisis to serve Singaporeans in need.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Cash strapped middle income families may be living in HDB or private properties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, I think that this issue may be addressed by proper analysis and implementing safeguards on the part of banks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are in arguably one of the most uncertain times in the history of mankind.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: No single government has been able to claim from the start they know how to navigate through the challenges posed by COVID-19 and the consequences it has brought to countries, cities, societies and economies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our Government of 55 years since our Independence is no exception.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Like everywhere else, the disruptions brought on by COVID-19 have unsettled businesses, lives and governments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a sign of things to come in the world, where no government can claim that their past experience will provide useful relevance for the uncertain future.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this brave new world, many heads with different ideas working out consensual solutions for the common good must be preferred.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will start on the issue of support for businesses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As most businesses stop receiving the 75% wage support coming out from the circuit breaker period, we may start to see a more accurate picture of businesses suffering and insolvency figures for companies rising later this year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unfortunately, to businesses who cannot open or operate or even for businesses who face a significant drop in their businesses at this time, it may not stave off business and cost pressures in a significant way.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In effect, it will be too small an amount to save ailing businesses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps the assistance by way of JSS and rental support could have been more targeted and not applied to businesses who may not be affected, for example, supermarkets or certain businesses in healthcare, pharmaceutical or IT sectors, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this way, more will be available to the businesses who need them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should not rely on unaffected businesses to voluntarily return their payouts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The announced support in the Fortitude Budget for digital transformation whether for purpose of boosting e-payments or the digital resilience bonus may help to promote e-payments and to allow safe management practices in COVID-19 settings.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While they may assist with business continuity under unique COVID-19 operating conditions, these schemes may be less helpful in generating business or revenue in themselves.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The financing support for promising start-ups under the Fortitude Budget may help some new start-ups but are probably irrelevant to the bulk of our existing SME businesses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Beyond the above-mentioned schemes, beyond the foreign work levy waivers and rebates announced in this Fortitude Budget, beyond the assistance from credit loans announced in previous budgets, I am concerned that many SME businesses will still require more assistance if we are to expect them to survive.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What are the Government's plans to support them to tide through the months or year ahead beyond what has been announced under the Fortitude Budget?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Has the Government factored in any actual draft plans in arriving at the additional $13 billion Contingencies Funds asked for in this Fortitude Budget and if so, whether it can now share such plans with Singaporeans too?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I next move on to the challenges during the circuit breaker and the issue of letting businesses open up with less restrictions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The circuit breaker has not been an easy period for many businesses and individuals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some businesses are baffled why similar businesses did not always result in the same exemptions or the same manpower allocation ratios.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instructions have changed over the weeks for some businesses ranging from meal arrangements for hawkers to types of businesses allowed to be opened or types of merchandise allowed to be sold.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the first few weeks of the circuit breaker, provision shops and minimarts in different Hougang precincts were given different directions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some were told they were only allowed to sell food.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some were told that they were not allowed to sell mops, brooms, brushes, pails, cleaning liquids, even slippers and limited stationery.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some were allowed to sell with no restrictions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Operators were baffled as some of these items have been sold in NTUC FairPrice without restrictions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thankfully, after the Hougang Member of Parliament sought clarifications, the authorities reached out and rectified the instructions given.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the circuit breaker period, most businesses were required to stop operating in their premises and most employees could not work in their working premises and had to stay at home.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those who could still do some or all of their work at home were the lucky few ones as for many jobs and many businesses, telecommuting is either not an option at all or not an adequate option for a variety of reasons.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many businesses have been looking forward to the resumption of operations in their premises.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, it has been somewhat confusing and uncertain for many business owners whose businesses were supposedly cleared for resumption.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Workers who need infrequent access to the workplace for information or materials can already do so on an existing time-based exemption...

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To continue with telecommuting per se may not be a viable option for many as telecommuting may suit certain positions but not others, and viable work that is required to be carried out in the office and unsuitability for telecommuting goes beyond the over-simplified description of merely requiring "the use of machinery and specialised terminals or need to complete legal documentation", especially bearing in mind many businesses will as I have highlighted earlier see their wage support under the JSS reduced to 25% from June onwards.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government can be less prescriptive in this area, including any current limitation in the number of workers allowed in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let businesses take ownership in managing telecommuting and the extent of telecommuting as appropriate for each individual business and their bottom line.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Where any of these employees are required to be in the office or for workers where telecommuting has limited application, the Government can leave the onus on businesses to carry out prescribed safe workplace practices, including having appropriate social distancing and safe seating arrangements, use of SafeEntry, keeping records of staff and visitors to premises, including temperature records and good cleaning practices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let businesses focus on recovery with more breathing space.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am sure that most businesses will understand that their business operations are subject to closure due to failure in social distancing and safe workplace arrangements or in the event of an actual infection and most will take the necessary protective steps accordingly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am asking these questions because pending a review of our labour policies in the near future – perhaps after the COVID-19 crisis, particularly on our current unhealthy level of reliance on cheap foreign labour and also the way we house them, in the meantime, we need these workers to be back helping to restart our economy and also at the end of the day, the workers do not ordinarily live and work outside of Singapore and they are part of our community.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am also asking these questions because it touches on how confident the Government is in bringing down infection in the foreign worker dormitories to zero.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I want to touch on safe connectivity with the world.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Prior to that, the Government had also announced that there will be talks to reopen borders with New Zealand.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Quite understandably, we cannot stay unconnected for too long and the opening up of air travel and connection with these and, indeed, other countries will be beneficial to our businesses and economy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, we have had recent experience of significant COVID-19 infections brought about by arriving passengers from abroad, first with the Wuhan tourists in January bringing the first recorded cases and transmissions to Singapore and then later on with some of those returning to Singapore or visitors from abroad around the period of March and April.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the Government's plans to open up air travel in the coming months even with selected countries and pending the eventual introduction of a vaccine for COVID-19, I hope that all necessary measures will be taken to ensure that the reopening will not lead to a resurgence of imported COVID-19 cases.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It has been reported that passengers will not be required to serve the 14-days quarantine period and they will be required to undertake swab tests before boarding and after arrival in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If swab tests are required before boarding a flight to Singapore, how do we ensure all overseas swab test results provided are reliable?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For swab tests done on arrival, how will the Government ensure that pending the outcome of the testing, there will not be any risk to any persons with whom the passengers come into contact at the airport, at their selected accommodation and also while being transported to their accommodation?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are there any restrictions on their accommodation for this initial period?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Besides being a potential Achilles' heel in our fight against COVID-19, it is inconsistent with social distancing efforts that were carried out previously on trains during the circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, we may start to see the number of business failures going up in the next few months, leading to more job losses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also hope that the Government will extend more flexibility to businesses who are cleared to resume business on their premises, to manage their businesses as they see fit as long as they comply with safe distancing and other safe workplace practices as required by the Government.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As for the Government’s plans to resume airlinks with China and New Zealand, it is important to resume connection for the benefit of our economy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I hope the Government will take all necessary measures to ensure that we will avoid another wave of foreign imported COVID-19 infections.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As more rail and bus services are resumed in phase 1, 2 and 3, I also hope that the Government take all necessary measures for safe travel and social distancing especially during peak hours.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I also want to thank the colleagues in MCCY and the National Arts Council (NAC) for their dedication and commitment to keep arts going strong.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: They work tirelessly to render support in this difficult period.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore Chinese Orchestra's digital efforts has seen six series, more than 130 contents uploaded, and a total of more than one million viewership to-date.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore Symphony Orchestra's SSOPlayOn! series, the Siong Leng Musical Association and the Nam Hwa Opera have brought their art onto several social media platforms for all to enjoy.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The theatre groups live-stream their performances and the Esplanade partners with SISTIC to provide pay-per-view tickets to achieve self-sustained model for online performances.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: In these difficult times, we need the arts and culture to uplift our spirits.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: One, cultivate concert virtual exposure acquired by the expanding digital consumers of arts to actual engagement.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Two, capability building should revamp and remodel in the strategic marketing area to bring headcounts for the various arts form, especially for ticketed events.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Three, digital culture pass to encourage pay-per-view digital concert and even purchasing of live concert tickets when we allow concert to be staged at the concert hall.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Four, more can be done to commission and collaborate with the private and public sector to utilise collective resources for the arts presentation in a more effective way.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Arts are the engines of togetherness and collective sense-making.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: A lost in cultural eco-system would be harder to re-cultivate than to restore anything.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, I would like to thank Deputy Prime Minister Heng and his team for always having the livelihood of artists and arts group in their heart.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The Government pays great attention to the arts and the cultural sector, making arts an indispensable spiritual nourishment during the outbreak.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: NAC and Lianhe Zaobao worked together to launch the Zaobao Recital Series comprising four online programmes, including Chinese music, vocals, classical chamber music and literature reciting.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Netizens have responded warmly to these online programmes.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The enhanced Job Support Scheme has enabled many art groups and artists to maintain their livelihood during the outbreak and continue to create artworks and surprises, so that people can continue to enjoy arts performances online.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: For example, Singapore Chinese Orchestra staged the Tutti Singapore percussion performance; Singapore Symphony Orchestra uploaded SSOPlayOn! series, and Singapore Chinese Music Federation gathered 30 Erhu players to present a performance called "Towards a Brighter Future" in celebration of the 30th anniversary of Singapore-China diplomatic ties.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Dingyi Music Company, Siong Leng Musical Association, Nan Hwa Opera and the Singapore Chinese Cultural Centre have also created many online stay-home performances.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: During this period, many enthusiastic supporters are paying special attention to the vulnerable groups by giving them donations and support.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I feel that freelancers in the arts and cultural sector will need our help too.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The existence of our local arts and cultural community is the spirit and hope of the society.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This group of people will not be the first to come to people's mind to help.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Their livelihood is not easy in the first place, and made worse by the outbreak.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The support they received is far from enough, and this reflects the fundamental cultural attitude of a society.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, we need a wider definition of arts and broader arts recognition among our people, so that more people are willing to support and promote arts and spread its values.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that artists and arts groups can make good use of the funding and grants in these difficult times, move on with fortitude and continue to innovate and create.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that the community will emerge stronger and more united after COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The development of arts and culture would also be different from before.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: We will need new engines and new concepts to create a new world.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I hope we can bring online audiences to concert halls and theatres.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: After artists have returned to the stage, I believe they will be able to create more inspiring programmes.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This is because arts can provide spiritual nourishments, lift people's mood and warm their hearts.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: We will definitely conquer COVID-19, start a new life accompanied by beautiful music and artistic creations, and unite as one people to march towards prosperity and progress.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We will need to meet these tests as one united people, united by our love for our country and one another Looking back, for me, the past two months have been extraordinary, working with Party colleagues and volunteers to provide support to residents remotely, adapting corporate processes to work from home and making adjustments to family life with my two young children, aged 12 and 14, going through home-based learning.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Now, our attention turns to the process of recovery.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is appropriate that an Emerging Stronger Task Force has been formed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I agree with the remarks made by my Party Chairman Ms Sylvia Lim on the composition and work of that task force.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a society, it is our collective responsibility to reflect, draw the right lessons and emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After all, the world went through the cataclysm of the Spanish flu in 1918 but many lessons about preventing and controlling pandemics were not permanently and widely institutionalised after that trauma.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What can we learn from this episode for this post-circuit breaker period and the post-COVID-19 future that Singapore will emerge into?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the start of the pandemic, the Government quickly formed a whole-of-Government task force and issued regular communications.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The challenge facing this task force was gargantuan.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our knowledge of COVID-19 was imperfect and evolving.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What followed was some confusion as those selling mainly cakes try to find out what they could do.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was clarified that they could sell their inventory of cakes but not bake new ones.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some bakeries, such as one making mainly croissants, had to clarify how the rules apply to them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Initially, when the circuit breaker was announced, motor workshops were told they could apply to stay open but only for emergency services.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A Straits Times' report from 7 April said that motor workshop operators were confused initially by the phrase "emergency vehicle services" found in the GoBusiness COVID-19 site.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do they mean emergency vehicles like ambulances or do they mean emergency services for vehicles, one asked.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another example, in late April it was announced that exercising and dog walking were not permitted within the common areas of condominiums.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One letter writer to TODAY on the 30 April mentioned that "to access public spaces, dogs would have to traverse the common condominium grounds thus rendering the rule moot in practice." Such a rule may also have had the effect of condominium dog owners then crowding in adjacent pathways by the road, HDB or landed common areas or parks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The intent behind these finely calibrated and frequently revised rules was good.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But in hindsight, could the technocratic zeal have been tempered by an appreciation that the capacity of society to adapt to so many frequently changing rules is not unlimited, while the capacity of any civil service to issue so many detailed and finely calibrated rules in a very short time is limited.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Too frequent and unclear rules can lead to rules fatigue and cynicism towards rule compliance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, would it not have been more efficient for the exceptions and caveats to rules to have been announced at the same time as the rule.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And could some rules that micro-manage what are permissible activities have been avoided in favour of making facility owners responsible for safe distancing, masking and so on?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, for example, in Phase One most retail, cinemas, bars, restaurants, event-based activities and tuition centres remain shut.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is in spite of the fact that crowds and lack of safe distancing have been anecdotally observed in a number of supermarket outlets and shopping malls under current rules, and that safe distancing is no longer mandatory on public transport.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to find the right balance between protecting livelihoods and protecting lives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means allowing most establishments to open may be with the exception of those which pose the most extreme risk.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But every establishment would be tasked to practise safe distancing, masking and other precautions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would mean that some establishments would, perhaps, not be able to optimise capacity to economically viable levels.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But should we not that choice to business owners?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some business owners may prefer to restart with reduced capacity so as to generate some cashflow, refresh connections with customers, start to rotate staff back to work for the sake of morale and skills refreshing and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For those industries where the risk is greater, these should be targeted for more enforcement and regular preventive COVID-19 testing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, the administration of rapid testing and swift isolation in a surgical manner, as opposed to only very severe lockdowns, has been seen as a key to Korea's success, which brings me to my next point on testing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Laboratory staff operating the extractors must also wear personal protective equipment or PPE and most countries looking to exit lockdown have similar mass testing strategies – increasing demand for the same reagents and PPE.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOH has said that coronavirus test were conducted by 13 laboratories in Singapore, the majority of which are located at public healthcare institutions such as hospitals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are private sector industrial testing labs that offer testing of COVID-19 on surfaces, not patient swabs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not clear if these labs currently also offer testing of human samples since this is not advertised.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would be good to know if these industrial labs can be co-opted to help with our testing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Tony Blair Institute in the UK has called for antibody tests to be more widely used in conjunction with the PCR test, even if it is less accurate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Could such antibody tests together with the current PCR test be used to triage testing of suspected cases to take the load off the PCR testing infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, Sir, a number of new schemes have been rolled out.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To cite some random examples – Workfare, Jobs Credit, Innovation Credit and SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some schemes are automatically applied and money gets transferred into your bank account.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some schemes you have to apply for to get the money or support.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For other schemes, the money exists in an account tagged to each citizen and you have to use it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, the more complex the whole system becomes the more resources need to go into the work of explaining, sifting through and helping people or firms to apply for these schemes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Social workers and Family Service Centres and officers at economic agencies like Enterprise Singapore, for example, would have to meet this challenge by mastering all the minutiae of the schemes and then explaining them well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Government consider a unified portal across the whole-of-Government where each citizen and company can log on, view and transact?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such a portal would show firstly, that the monies that have been credited from all schemes that automatically kick in; two, the schemes which that person or company is eligible to apply for; or where there is imperfect information where they may be eligible to apply for for those that need application with direct links to the application forms from respective Ministries, Statutory Boards and agencies; and thirdly, the money that has been credited to them in special accounts but which needs to be utilised by a certain date.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The existence of such a portal would be a first step.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The next step would be to streamline the schemes and curb the tendency to launch new schemes but attempt instead to channel support into existing schemes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And in saying this, for the elderly who are less IT-savvy, arrangements need to be made to facilitate their access to such a portal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And what incentives were used to secure these investments?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is important to continue to attract FDI and to refine and improve our strategies for doing so.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the economic challenge of developing home-grown entrepreneurship and our own world-beating companies is going to be greater than ever.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: World trade growth was already slowing own even before COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: COVID-19 will not put in an end to FDI for sure.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But it is likely to result in more competition for perhaps less FDI, as some multi-national companies or MNCs migrate some operations back home and other MNCs try to diversify to less traditional FDI destinations, responding to the imperatives of supply chain resilience, political pressures and other imperatives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: No doubt there are many schemes and programmes to stimulate entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this House my colleagues and I have mooted a number of ideas on this front in the past.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, setting up a fund to support ex-civil servants who want to become entrepreneurs and demonstrating more flexibility in schemes based on results.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Uplifting our entrepreneurial sector is going to be a key national competitiveness challenge facing Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would argue for renewed soul searching and efforts on this front as an urgent priority.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Malay):   The Government's approach to Phase One and beyond hinges on the demarcation of companies into either an essential or non-essential category for each phase.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is in spite of the fact that crowds have been observed to continue visiting a number of supermarkets in shopping centres and are not really practising safe distancing under current rules.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Has the Government considered an alternative approach, which is to calibrate this a little less finely, but in a broader manner instead?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means allowing most businesses to open, perhaps with the exception of those which may pose the most extreme risks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, every business should be required to practise safe distancing, the wearing of masks and all other precautions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And for those industries where the risk is greater, these should be targeted for more enforcement and regular, preventive COVID-19 testing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, has COVID-19 shown that our model of economics and politics is perfect?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And so, in conclusion, Mr Speaker, Sir, at the end of this speech, I find myself returning to a theme in my very first speech in this House given in January 2016 – the Singapore glass is half full.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What would happen after the deployment of significant reserves to support lives and livelihoods?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I also spoke about how COVID-19 had exposed inequalities – how the wages of some Singaporeans working in essential services need to go up – and what opportunities the COVID-19 crisis had engendered to reimagine a better Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For this Fortitude Budget debate, which once again calls for a draw on the reserves, I will focus on three "E"s – the economy, engagement and empathy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the central focus of this Budget was jobs, Deputy Prime Minister Heng's speech was instructive in my view for the restatement of three hard truths in the coming months.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, Singapore can expect some tough times ahead.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, the Deputy Prime Minister reminded Singaporeans that life will not return to pre-COVID-19 days, with the global economy unlikely to recover quickly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This has hitherto been significantly supported by the Jobs Support Scheme (JSS).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With poor economic growth at the door, some business owners have shared with me that they have retained workers as long as they could, thanks to the JSS, even as other workers were emplaced on no-pay leave and have had to take pay cuts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, the goal of the Government to accelerate digitalisation, up-skilling for the future and the creation of a National Jobs Council are steps in the right direction and supported by the Workers' Party.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These initiatives cohere with an eye on the future and the transformation to a post-COVID-19-ready Singapore economy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Today, some Singaporeans would be downcast at the thought of how to finance or how to continue financing their mortgage and other commitments, or the opportunities they can or cannot provide to their school-going children when their own paychecks have dwindled or, in other cases, evaporated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On mid-career workers, I hope the Government considers and incentivises more companies and businesses, through either rebates or reliefs, to offer more of such traineeships and opportunities to mid-career Singaporeans, so that they can learn new skills and embark on new careers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Unlike the Resilience Budget, I noticed the Fortitude Budget did not include a line to say that the Government would be prepared to make further draws on past Reserves to deal with COVID-19, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Nonetheless, I have a few questions for the Deputy Prime Minister on this count.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would appear that this Contingencies Fund would provide the Government with a significant buffer against post-circuit breaker uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What is of interest is the decision-making process behind the allocation of this amount.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And on what basis was it justified to the President?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is a very significant comment on Singapore's fiscal health, the implications of which have not been discussed in public in a significant way thus far.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Deputy Prime Minister share more details on his thinking on this matter and what can the public expect in the short and medium term over the next five to 10 years, especially with regard to recurrent taxes and the social contract between people and the state.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This brings me to my second "E" – engagement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party has not come in to publicly criticise the Government on its handling of an unprecedented crisis in ways that would undermine the national effort.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But Singaporeans have a right to expect a thorough review and accounting on the response to this public health crisis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some, both in and out of this House, have suggested a commission of inquiry or some other independent body to review specific aspects of the Government's response thus far.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Whatever the form such a reckoning takes in future, our position, as a constructive Opposition, requires us to communicate the feelings of Singaporeans on the ground in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As we exit the circuit breaker, there is the perception that the Government's handling of the COVID-19 crisis has certainly not included adjectives more commonly associated with the Singapore Government, such as clarity and decisiveness.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, there is a broadly accepted view that the public should have been told early and clearly, and not through illegal recordings behind closed doors, for example, that universal masking would prove to be a challenge in view of supply constraints requiring the Government to prioritise our healthcare and other essential workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For some Singaporean businesses, at times, it felt as if no one in Government was taking ownership of how COVID-19 directives would be perceived, interpreted and understood on the ground.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Then, they were higher order trade-offs and decisions that could have turned very differently in view of numerous unknowns associated with the spread of the virus.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While other countries requisitioned mask supply lines, it would appear that Singapore resisted doing so, probably with an eye on the future so that international companies would always see Singapore as a reliable place to do business.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But rather than getting the public to speculate about these decision making trade-offs, such as whether the possible shortage of reagents to ramp up COVID-19 testing far more quickly was a problem, the public was largely left to infer positions that ought to have been unequivocally made by the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For younger Singaporeans, this crisis has been educational and revealing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: COVID-19 has reinforced for some Singaporeans, if not exposed for others, especially younger Singaporeans, how reliant Singapore is on foreign sources of manpower and supplies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is something commentators online would do well to remember when they speak ill or run down our neighbours.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can we imagine the psychological impact on Singapore had Malaysia stopped food supplies like vegetables as well?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A belated explanation of Singapore having raised its DORSCON level to Orange in 2009 as a result of H1N1, ostensibly to temper panic-buying, and the jolting of memories about the existence of a rice stockpile could not overcome a distinct lack of understanding and preparedness about emergencies amongst many segments of the public.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is unlike the mindset of many Merdeka and Pioneer Generation Singaporeans who would recall emergency preparedness exercises, such as water rationing, for example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Engaging more Singaporeans on the need to better compensate for, if not overcome, our limitations in key areas and reintroducing public emergency preparedness for psychological resilience, has been exposed by the crisis, and significant focus would need to be placed on this in future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such a thorough review could potentially become a source of more job opportunities for Singaporeans, pegged at more respectable wage levels in some cases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope this is something the National Jobs Council can look at.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The last "E" I wish to talk about is empathy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We have experienced it in bucket loads over the last two months – a greater acknowledgement of mental health issues; warm cheers of support for healthcare frontliners from HDB flats and condominiums; more stories of Singaporeans offering the Food Panda or Grab delivery person water or a drink before he or she fulfils the next order; and the list goes on.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans may have grumbled, but they got on with their lives in spite of the inconveniences of the circuit breaker and played their part in protecting lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, many younger Singaporeans have taken a great interest in those less well-off.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This has been one of the seminal moments of the COVID-19 experience thus far.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Volunteering to help distribute food to Singaporeans in need, volunteering to swab foreign workers, delivering laptops to families in need with school-going children, and so much more.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In a crisis that this generation of Singaporeans will never forget, we saw the best of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And empathy is a significant source from which fortitude springs and a basis to call upon the cohesion and strength needed for Singapore to overcome challenges and odds.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In response to my Resilience Budget speech and, specifically the reference to the New Deal in the US, Deputy Prime Minister Heng cautioned about localising schisms from the US where liberals support comprehensive relief and reform programmes, and conservatives oppose plans that are hostile to growth and business.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister would be aware that Singapore is not alien to diametrically opposed ideological perspectives and these have been present in Singapore for some time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The online discourse has, in fact, accentuated it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Another case in point is the recent response of various Chambers of Commerce on the calls made by Singaporeans to moderate the number of foreign workers in Singapore as a result of the COVID-19 experience.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With many corporates and big businesses already perceived to be over-represented in our political ecology, be it through the grassroots or through their association in private-public national level committees, the Government needs to consider how it can become a better arbiter between different views, to give and encourage more space to our youths, NGOs unlinked to GLCs and trade unions, and the people sector to voice their contrarian views and perspectives.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This should be done while retaining a laser-like focus on fact-based conversations that portend a progressive future all Singaporeans can endeavour towards.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, we have some Singaporeans, including young ones, wondering whether we had done right by foreign workers, calling for an improvement of their living conditions, but only to be met by naysayers questioning their motives.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, COVID-19 has, paradoxically, vindicated a smaller group of Singaporeans who have been lobbying for improvements to foreign worker management policies for years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In my view, Mr Speaker, we should count ourselves fortunate that we have citizens who are the loving critics amongst us, some of whom have been questioned in this very House in this term of Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Members would recall one citizen's poems were nitpicked with a view to cast wholly negative aspersions on his character, even though that individual was not present in the House to defend himself.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If binary black-and-white perspectives are the shape of how we as a society deal with differences after COVID-19, Singapore will become an ordinary society, no different from many around the world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But nobody expects the Government to willy-nilly change its decision at the first sign of pressure and agree with a critic.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans do recognise the multitude of perspectives the Government has to take cognisance of, but it is important to recognise and not forget that citizens criticise and even organise, because they care.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As we traverse the post-COVID-19 volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous (VUCA) world, we need to place more faith and promote even greater participation from Singaporeans than ever before.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I use the word "pivot" because Singapore is a far more complex and varied economy and society than it was in 1965.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Kudos to the Government and especially the MOF team who stitched the Budgets together.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has caused more disruption than one can imagine – changing lives and livelihoods as we knew them to be.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Economic activities have plummeted, the depth and speed of which rival that of the Great Depression.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Experts worldwide cannot agree on how long the downturn will be.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is no telling what the recovery is going to look like – V-curve, U-curve, Z-curve, a smooth bounce-back, a slow-burn recovery or worse still, a relapse.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One of Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong's favourite quotes during this season is by former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill who said this, "Now, this is not the end.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not even the beginning of the end.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But it is perhaps, the end of the beginning".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Indeed, change has only begun even as Singapore exits from the circuit breaker.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many people, businesses and individuals, understandably are very concerned about how this recovery will look like.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I therefore seek Deputy Prime Minister and MOF's reading of the pace of recovery and what the overall strategy would look like in the best case scenario and in the worst case scenario.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I want to move next to touch on two things.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One, on the small and medium enterprises or SMEs; and two, on charities, the social service sector and the disabled.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We all know that the SMEs form an integral part of Singapore's economic landscape, embodying the spirit of entrepreneurship of our nation and employing more than two-thirds of our local workforce.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I applaud the Singapore Government's and especially MTI's relentless efforts in supporting them, even before the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: SMEs with a headstart and stronger technological capabilities are likely to recover faster from the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The prognosis of the rest of the economy will be uncertain.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, using a simple segmentation based on one's willingness to change and two, the ability to change, there appears to be four groups of SMEs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The first group: those who are willing and able to change.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I think they will benefit most from Government schemes and they include the early adopters and the high-potential start-ups that are targeted in the Budget.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How will we facilitate this group more to help them scale further and to open more doors for and with them?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Group two: those who are able to change and not willing to change.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How do we convince and incentivise them so more of them will come on board?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Group three: those who are not able to change and not willing to change.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I think we have no choice but to let them exit.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But how will we, considering that they are also Singapore SMEs, how will we help them exit with a softer landing?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The last group, which is likely the largest, those who are willing to change but not able to change for various reasons.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is the largest group for which the strategy has to be training and coaching.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a need, a real need to make them not just "apprentices" and also "disciples" so that more of them can sustain digitalisation efforts and continue to be successful as we emerge from the crisis.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Is there some way by which we can invest and handhold them longer and deeper?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Pair them perhaps with not just simply Digitalisation Ambassadors, but Digitalisation Coaches who can equip them with more and deeper operational and systemic skills and knowledge in such areas like backend stock inventory management, customer fulfilment, digital marketing skills and so forth.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And finally, for those who eventually have to cease operations but nonetheless have the acumen and energy to continue, can there be, for the SMEs, an equivalent of a "professional-conversion" scheme, just like what we have for individuals, a placement scheme, to help them seize business or job opportunities in sectors that are more in the sunrise spaces like urban farming, logistics, warehousing, healthcare, estate maintenance and so forth?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, I want to move from business to the charities, social service sector and the disabled.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The services range from serving the elderly to the young, families, they operate in nursing homes, day activity centres, family service centres, early intervention to special education schools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have several suggestions for consideration by Government for this sector and for the people served by the sector.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And fundraising provides a substantial top up to Government grants and subsidies for them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Suggestion two: for this sector is to target high needs areas.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are groups with high support needs which call for more attention and resourcing so that they are not left behind.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Suggestion three: can we include more blatantly, more explicitly and visibly charities and the social service sector in the transformation masterplan of Singapore?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Transformation of a nation is needed – not just in the business sector but also in the not-for-profit sector.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of the push for digitalisation, innovation and entrepreneurship in business are relevant to the people sector.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The willing amongst them, like the SMEs, require not only just Digital Ambassadors but also digital coaches and partners.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Charities with high potential and good track records, should be facilitated and governed with a lighter touch.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Let them thrive, let them push the boundaries to greater heights and support them in their transformation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Suggestion four: include vulnerable groups such as the disabled right at the start of planning in all of the good things: the digitalistion, jobs and skills upgrading movement, including and not limited to the exciting plans for the new National Jobs Council, SG-United Jobs and Traineeship and SkillsFuture efforts.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, adopt the principle of what is commonly known now as universal design and design for all, right at the start.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: BCA and MND have already done so in the design of buildings and the physical built environment.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The same should be applied in other areas as well in the protection and creation of jobs an skills upgrading.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is no secret that jobs are already hard to come by for persons with disabilities during normal times.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us not give up easily on those who are willing to change but not able to change for some reasons, whether they are SMEs, social service agencies, our elderly, our disabled or others who are vulnerable in our Singapore family.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They say it takes a globe to fight this pandemic.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And indeed, the globe includes us and it starts with each one of us.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Once again, I quote Winston Churchill who said, "These are not dark days these are great days... we must all thank God that we have been allowed, each of us according to our stations to play a part in making these days memorable in the history of our race." And I want to end off with a quote by our founding father of Singapore, Mr Lee Kuan Yew, of whom I know Deputy Prime Minister Heng is a great fan.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
